senses.definition: Ease off from a fierce or troubling level, or bring something down from such a level.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To calm down after being at its worst.

examples.text: Her fear began to abate once the plane leveled off and the shaking stopped.
The hospital hired extra nurses for flu season and let them go once the rush of patients abated.
The mediator's slow, calm questions helped abate the tension in the room.
The rush for concert tickets abated after the first hour, and the website stopped crashing.

distractors.lemma: Play the accomplice in someone else's misdeed.
Hand over a crown or other high office by stepping down from it.
Grovel so low before others that one's pride is lost.
Scuff or scratch away the top layer of something through rough contact.

mnemonics: Abate comes from Old French abatre, to knock down: something that abates has been knocked down from its full strength.

senses.definition: Markedly different from an accepted norm.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wandering off from what is normal or expected.

examples.text: For a man who had paid every bill on time for forty years, skipping three months of rent was so aberrant that his landlord called his daughter.
Shouting at a reporter was aberrant behavior for a diplomat known for thirty years of perfect calm.
The algorithm flags aberrant spending patterns to protect consumers from fraudulent charges.
Bird watchers were puzzled by the aberrant flight of a flock of geese heading north in the middle of autumn.

distractors.lemma: Vile enough to provoke loathing in anyone who sees it.
Being a perfect example of something bad, with nothing to soften it.
Plain to anyone who looks, needing no explanation.
Grating and harsh toward others, so that people bristle.
Plentiful to the point of overflowing.

mnemonics: The word aberrant contains err, reminding you of behavior that errs from the standard path.

senses.definition: Disappear on the quiet to dodge arrest or repayment, often with someone else's cash.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To run off in secret, often with stolen money, so you will not get caught.

examples.text: Before the police could serve the warrant, the suspect managed to abscond across the border.
The wedding planner absconded with the couple's deposit, and her office was empty by the following Monday.
The lodger absconded in the night, leaving three months of unpaid rent and a note on the kitchen table.
Rather than face trial for fraud, the developer absconded to a country with no extradition treaty.

distractors.lemma: Declare someone free of a sin or charge, lifting the burden of guilt.
Move upward toward a summit or a higher floor.
Occur so plentifully that one meets it at every turn.
Deny oneself something tempting, by personal choice.

mnemonics: Abscond comes from Latin abscondere, to hide away: someone who absconds slips off and hides, often with the money.

senses.definition: Go without a pleasure on purpose, for a while or for good.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say no to a treat or habit by your own choice.

examples.text: She has abstained from buying new clothes for a whole year, mending and swapping instead.
Members of the recovery group pledge to abstain from betting of any kind, even office pools.
The monks abstain from speech until after the morning meal.
Hoping to save for a house, the couple abstained from restaurant meals and holidays for two years.

distractors.lemma: Pardon someone, wiping a wrong from their record.
Take a spill or other liquid up into its fibers.
Boil a long report down to its main points.
Hang on to something that might otherwise slip away.
Prop up an effort so it does not flag or fade.

senses.definition: Let a vote pass without counting oneself on either side.

mnemonics: Abstain comes from Latin abs-, away, and tenere, to hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away from something.

senses.definition: Call out someone's misbehavior and caution them against doing it again, usually without anger.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give someone a serious talking-to about what they did wrong.

examples.text: The librarian admonished the teenagers for talking loudly in the quiet reading room.
The flight attendant admonished the passenger for unbuckling his seatbelt while the sign was still lit.
My grandmother would gently admonish us whenever we forgot to thank the cook.
After the referee admonished him for a rough tackle, the player kept his temper for the rest of the match.

distractors.lemma: Leave someone open-mouthed at an event far beyond what they thought possible.
Tear an argument apart so thoroughly that nothing of it stands.
Top up a stock that has run low so there is enough again.
Wipe a rule or custom off the books for good.
Feel a glow of respect for someone's gifts or deeds.

senses.definition: Give someone a sober word of caution before they act.

mnemonics: Admonish shares a Latin root with monitor: monere, to warn. To admonish someone is to warn them about their conduct.

senses.definition: Cut a food, drink or drug with a lesser ingredient and pass the result off as pure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To sneak a cheap or bad ingredient into food, drink or medicine.

examples.text: Dealers often adulterate street drugs with look-alike powders, which makes each dose dangerously unpredictable.
The roaster was caught adulterating its 'pure Kona' coffee with cheaper beans from other regions.
The assay showed that the 'pure gold' coins had been adulterated with copper and lead.
Some old-time bakers adulterated their flour with chalk to make loaves look whiter and weigh more.

distractors.lemma: Treat someone as a hero beyond all reason, praising every move they make.
Lay out a plan in broad strokes and leave the specifics for later.
Erase or flatten something until it can no longer be seen or recognized.
Hear both sides of a conflict and hand down a binding ruling.

mnemonics: Adulterate comes from Latin adulterare, to corrupt, a close relative of adultery: both spoil something that should stay pure.

senses.definition: Bearing on the beauty or artistic quality of something, as judged by taste.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having to do with beauty and how good something looks.

examples.text: The judges scored each garden on how healthy the plants were and on the aesthetic effect of the overall design.
The town insisted on burying the power lines, calling the poles an aesthetic blight on the old main street.
Her aesthetic instincts showed in the quilt, where every color and stitch seemed placed to please the eye.
Typographers argue over fonts on aesthetic grounds, debating which letters look most graceful on the page.

distractors.lemma: Choosing a bare, comfortless way of life as a form of discipline.
Unmoved by matters that would stir most people to care.
Deadening the nerves so that a patient feels nothing during treatment.
Produced by chemists as a stand-in for a natural material.

senses.definition: Attractive and stylish in a carefully chosen way.

mnemonics: Aesthetic goes back to Greek aisthanesthai, to perceive with the senses; anesthetic, from the same root, means without feeling.

senses.definition: Make a person or group mightier, or puff up their image beyond what is true.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To build up how powerful or famous someone is, or to make them seem bigger than they are.

examples.text: The dictator renamed the capital's main square after himself, one more way to aggrandize his rule.
Rather than aggrandize his own role, the coach gave the players full credit for the championship.
The ambitious duke married his daughters into royal families to aggrandize his house and widen its lands.
The town's founder ordered a statue of himself twice life size, a clear attempt to aggrandize his place in local history.

distractors.lemma: Deepen the damage of something that was already going badly.
Lump separate entries together and treat them as one.
Torment oneself at length over which way to go on a hard choice.
Keep stirring up public pressure until those in charge change course.
Do someone an injustice that leaves them bitter.

mnemonics: Aggrandize contains grand, from Latin grandis, large: to aggrandize someone is to make them grander in power or in show.

senses.definition: A brisk, willing response to a task or request, with no hint of holding back.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being quick and happy to do something as soon as you are asked.

examples.text: The young apprentice tackled even the dullest chores with surprising alacrity, never needing to be asked twice.
The waiter, hoping for a big tip, refilled our glasses with an alacrity we had not seen all evening.
My son, who takes an hour to unload the dishwasher, showed remarkable alacrity when his friends honked outside.
The dog bounded to the door with alacrity the moment its owner picked up the leash.

distractors.lemma: Crispness of expression that leaves a reader in no doubt.
Riotous fun that leaves people doubled over.
A sour, biting edge that creeps into every word once goodwill is gone.
Fineness of perception that catches small details others miss.

mnemonics: Alacrity comes from Latin alacer, lively and eager, the same root as allegro, the music term for a quick, bright pace.

senses.definition: Take some of the weight off a pain or hardship without removing its cause.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To take some of the sting out of pain or hardship.

examples.text: Shade sails over the playground alleviated the worst of the afternoon heat, though the slide still got warm.
A grant for textbooks alleviated the cost of college for her family, but tuition still meant years of loans.
Emergency wells alleviated the drought's toll on the villages until the rains returned.
New ramps alleviated some of the trouble wheelchair users had getting around the old campus.

distractors.lemma: Prop or hoist something to a greater height.
Cut a long word or name down to a few letters that stand for it.
Divide up money or resources and earmark each part for a set use.
Drive away people's goodwill so that former allies keep their distance.
Put forward a charge or claim that still awaits proof.

mnemonics: Alleviate comes from the Latin levis, meaning light, as in levity: to alleviate a pain is to make it lighter to carry.

senses.definition: Fuse separate organizations or substances into a single unit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To merge separate groups or things into one.

examples.text: After years of rivalry, the two hiking clubs amalgamated, pooling their dues and printing a single trail map.
Over the centuries, the dialects of the valley amalgamated into one language that kept words from all of them.
The bakers' and brewers' guilds, long at odds, finally amalgamated and elected a single master.
Gold miners once amalgamated gold dust with mercury, then heated the mix to drive the mercury off and leave pure metal.

distractors.lemma: Bring about an upturn in a poor state of affairs.
Radiate outward from the place where it starts.
Take a successful person as a pattern and set out to measure up to them.
Bring a dull scene or face to life with spirit and movement.

mnemonics: Amalgamate comes from amalgam, the blend of mercury and other metals long used to fill teeth: to amalgamate is to blend things into one.

senses.definition: Leaving a reader or listener unsure which of several possible senses the speaker had in mind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Leaving you guessing, because it could mean one thing or another.

examples.text: 'I saw the man with the telescope' is ambiguous, since either I had the telescope or he did.
Because the will was ambiguous about whether 'my children' included her stepson, the family ended up in court.
The sign's ambiguous arrow pointed between two roads, and half the drivers took the wrong one.
Her text, 'Fine, do what you want,' was so ambiguous that he could not tell whether she was angry.

distractors.lemma: Pulled two ways in feeling about a person or plan.
Hungry for success and prepared to push hard for it.
Having no weaker hand, so that either one serves for any task.
Fit for travel or life both ashore and in water.
Present in the general surroundings rather than coming from one source.

senses.definition: Not fitting neatly into one category, so its status stays unsettled.

mnemonics: Ambiguous starts with Latin ambi-, on both sides: an ambiguous remark leans both ways at once.

senses.definition: Divided in one's attitude toward something, because parts of it appeal and parts of it repel.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Part of you likes something and part of you does not, so you cannot make up your mind.

examples.text: She was ambivalent about selling her late father's piano; it took up half the room, yet she could not bear to see it go.
Longtime fans are ambivalent about the band's new album, admiring its polish while missing the rough edge of the early records.
He has an ambivalent relationship with his hometown, which he both misses and avoids visiting.
The review was ambivalent, praising the actors while calling the plot a mess.

distractors.lemma: Moved by goodwill to help others, without expecting anything back.
Full of spite and glad when harm comes to others.
Met with so often in a given setting that it seems to be the rule.
Able to stand in for another thing because the two come to the same amount or result.
Facing danger or hardship without backing down.

mnemonics: Ambivalent joins the Latin ambi-, 'both', with valere, 'to be strong': two opposite feelings pull with equal strength.

senses.definition: Bring a poor or painful state of affairs up to a better one.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make a hard situation less bad for the people in it.

examples.text: A ramp at the side entrance ameliorated the daily struggle of wheelchair users, who until then had been carried up the steps.
The talks did not settle the border dispute, but a prisoner exchange helped ameliorate relations between the two governments.
Nothing the landlord did could ameliorate the damp, cold conditions in the basement apartment.
Moving the night shift's start back an hour did a little to ameliorate the nurses' exhaustion, though the ward stayed short-staffed.

distractors.lemma: Bring separate firms or groups under one name and one management.
Mark the anniversary or legacy of a past person or event in a public way.
Go back over a point and fill it out at greater length.
Spend time going over the arguments on each side before choosing.
Wear down a debt on a set schedule, with each installment covering interest and part of the sum owed.

mnemonics: Ameliorate contains the Latin melior, meaning better: to ameliorate a bad situation is to make it better.

senses.definition: Something located at a time when it could not have existed or occurred.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that appears in the wrong historical era.

examples.text: A smartphone appearing in a nineteenth-century period drama is a glaring anachronism.
Viewers quickly spotted the anachronism of a Roman soldier wearing a wristwatch in the battle scene.
The novel contains an anachronism: a character in 1910 watches television, which had not yet been invented.
Fact-checkers flagged an anachronism in the script, since the song the hero hums was written thirty years after the story takes place.

distractors.lemma: The political view that people should live without any state or ruling authority.
Ongoing hostility between people or groups who work against each other.
An idea or practice so hateful to a group that its members reject it on sight.
A long account of a kingdom's or family's past, told one year after another.

senses.definition: A person, custom or object that seems out of date, as if left over from an earlier age.

mnemonics: Anachronism contains the Greek chronos, 'time', as in chronology: an anachronism is something placed in the wrong time.

senses.definition: Parallel to another thing in structure or role, even where the two differ in other respects.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Like something else in some ways, though different in others.

examples.text: The heart is analogous to a pump, since both push fluid through a network of pipes.
Some engineers see city traffic as analogous to blood flow, with jams acting like clots in an artery.
The lawyers searched for an analogous case from the past, one close enough to guide the judge.
Pruning a hedge is analogous to editing a draft: in both, you cut away growth so the shape underneath shows.

distractors.lemma: Standing apart from the rest of a set in a way that raises questions.
Unsigned or uncredited, so that its source stays a mystery.
Holding the final say over its own course, whatever any parent body might prefer.
Settled by a vote in which the whole group sided the same way.
Approaching a question by testing its parts with logic rather than relying on instinct.

senses.definition: In biology, of body parts in different species, serving the same purpose though they evolved separately.

mnemonics: Analogous comes from the Greek analogos, 'in due proportion', the source of analogy too: analogous things line up well enough that you can draw an analogy between them.

senses.definition: A case that does not match what the rest of its group or the usual rules would predict.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: One thing that is out of step with all the others.

examples.text: A single blue tile in an otherwise all-white floor was an anomaly that the builders never explained.
The only anomaly in her spotless driving record was one parking ticket from 2009.
The researchers ran the test again to see whether the strange reading was a real anomaly or a faulty sensor.
After eleven months of steady growth, the sharp drop in March looked like an anomaly rather than a trend.

distractors.lemma: The fact of going unnamed, so that one's words or deeds cannot be traced back.
A likeness drawn between two different things to carry an argument from one to the other.
The field that charts every bone, organ and vessel inside a body.
The standing of a person or region that answers to no master but itself.
Rancor between people that has grown open and hard to hide.

senses.definition: In astronomy, an angle giving a planet's position along its orbit, counted from its closest approach to the sun.

mnemonics: Anomaly comes from the Greek an- (not) and homalos (even or regular), meaning it does not follow the normal pattern.

senses.definition: A strong and settled aversion that sets one against a certain person or thing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep dislike of someone or something that makes you want to stay away.

examples.text: Her antipathy toward flattery made her distrust any salesperson who praised her taste.
Despite her antipathy toward long meetings, she sat through the three-hour budget review without complaint.
His antipathy to cats was so strong that he crossed the street to avoid one.
The senator's antipathy to new taxes was well known, so nobody expected her to back the fuel levy.

distractors.lemma: Indifference so deep that even pressing matters fail to stir any response.
Mind-to-mind contact, if it exists, in which one person knows another's unspoken thoughts.
The thing that stands at the opposite extreme from another.
Fellow feeling that lets one read and mirror another person's mood.

senses.definition: A person or thing that someone cannot stand.

mnemonics: Antipathy mirrors sympathy: both end in Greek pathos, 'feeling', but sympathy starts with syn-, 'together', and antipathy with anti-, 'opposed'.

senses.definition: Emotional flatness that leaves a person unmoved and unwilling to get involved.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not caring about something, and so not bothering to do anything about it.

examples.text: By the third week of the strike, anger had given way to apathy, and few workers bothered to show up at the picket line.
The coach was frustrated by the team's apathy; nobody seemed to care whether they won or lost.
After months of bad news, a kind of apathy set in, and she stopped even opening her bills.
The petition met with apathy, as most shoppers walked past without even glancing at it.

distractors.lemma: An ingrained hostility toward some person or thing.
Gradual loss of size and strength in a limb or organ that is left idle.
The heartbreaking strain in a film or tale that leaves viewers misty-eyed.
The claimed knack of reading another person's thoughts from across a room or a continent.

mnemonics: Apathy is the Greek a-, 'without', plus pathos, 'feeling': apathy is a state without feeling or interest.

senses.definition: Buy calm from an angry or threatening party by handing over part of what it wants.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say yes to some demands so an angry person will back off.

examples.text: The airline tried to appease the stranded passengers with meal vouchers and free hotel rooms.
Nothing the manager said could appease the furious customer whose order had been ruined.
The club's owner fired the coach to appease fans who had booed the team for weeks.
To appease the neighbors who had complained about the noise, the band agreed to stop rehearsing after nine.

distractors.lemma: Put a price on a property or valuable after inspecting it.
Lay hands on a fugitive and take them in.
Keep someone up to date by passing on what one knows.
Put an extra section after the main body of a report or file.
Take a lost case to a higher court in hope of a new verdict.

senses.definition: Take the edge off a hunger or craving for a time.

mnemonics: Appease has peace inside it, from the Old French pais, 'peace': you appease an angry person to restore the peace.

senses.definition: So hard and long that finishing it calls for stamina and grit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Needing so much effort that it wears you out.

examples.text: The refit of the old ship was arduous: crews spent two winters scraping, cutting and replacing every rusted plate by hand.
Rebuilding the town after the flood was an arduous task that took volunteers most of a year.
She called the bar exam the most arduous test of her life, after months of daily study.
Translating the ancient poem was arduous work, since every line had to be checked against three dictionaries.

distractors.lemma: Wholehearted and eager, with enthusiasm that runs hot.
Parched and cracked from years of scant rainfall.
Doubling back on itself at every turn instead of heading straight to its end.
Posing a threat to safety that calls for warnings and care.

mnemonics: Arduous comes from the Latin arduus, 'steep': an arduous task feels like a long climb up a steep hill.

senses.definition: Express an idea or emotion in exact and orderly language.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To put an idea into words so plainly that others get it.

examples.text: Poets often articulate what the rest of us feel but cannot put into words.
The founder articulated the company's values so clearly that new hires can recite them after a day.
A strong essay articulates one main argument and backs it up with evidence.
Therapy helped him articulate feelings he had kept to himself for years.

distractors.lemma: Talk with one's hands, waving them about as one speaks.
Be entered on a college's register as one of its students.
Hear both sides of a quarrel and hand down a binding decision.
Toss around theories about what might be true when proof is lacking.
Flow round and round through a set of pipes or vessels.

senses.definition: Pronounce every syllable crisply and distinctly.

mnemonics: Articulate comes from the Latin articulus, 'small joint': to articulate a thought is to lay it out in clear, separate parts, like the segments of a finger.

senses.definition: Refusing ease and pleasure as a discipline, in the belief that hardship trains the spirit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living very simply and refusing comforts and pleasures on purpose.

examples.text: During Lent he kept an ascetic diet of bread, lentils and water, and slept on a thin mat.
The marathon runner's ascetic habits (no sugar, no alcohol, bed by nine) struck her friends as joyless.
He gave up his car and his phone in an ascetic attempt to simplify his life.

distractors.lemma: Concerned with taste and whether something is pleasing to look at.
Containing the sour acid that vinegar is made of.
Kept sterile so that no infection can be passed on.
Holding that there is no god at all.

mnemonics: Ascetic comes from the Greek askesis, "exercise": an ascetic trains the body to do without comforts.

senses.definition: Ease a painful or unwelcome feeling, such as guilt, fear or grief, so that it troubles someone less.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To ease a bad feeling, such as worry or guilt.

examples.text: The surgeon's calm, step-by-step explanation did much to assuage the parents' fears about the operation.
He sent flowers and a long apology, hoping to assuage his guilt over forgetting her birthday.
Nothing the coach said could assuage the team's disappointment after losing the final in overtime.
Years went by, but time did little to assuage her grief over the loss of her brother.

distractors.lemma: Talk someone out of a plan or course of action.
Rush at an enemy and strike at them again and again.
Size up a person, plan or problem and reach a verdict on its merits.
Treat something as a fact before anyone has shown it to be one.

senses.definition: Satisfy a need of the body, such as thirst or hunger.
Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.

mnemonics: Assuage goes back to Latin suavis, sweet, the root of suave: to assuage a bitter feeling is to sweeten it.

senses.definition: Daring enough to try something risky that most people would not attempt.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very bold and ready to take big chances.

examples.text: The explorer devised an audacious plan to cross the Antarctic continent alone on foot.
In an audacious move, the tiny startup offered to buy the company that had once turned its founders away.
The thieves pulled off an audacious robbery in broad daylight, strolling out of the museum past two guards.
Down by a goal with seconds left, the striker tried an audacious shot from the halfway line.

distractors.lemma: Possible to hear, even if only faintly.
Driven by an endless craving to pile up wealth.
Showing deep wisdom and sound judgment.
Regularly dishonest, with a habit of saying what is false.

senses.definition: Unrestrained by convention or propriety.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Disrespectfully bold and showing no regard for normal rules or manners.

examples.text: The junior clerk made an audacious demand for an immediate partnership during his annual review.
Critics condemned the playwright for his audacious disregard of historical facts.
Such audacious behavior at a solemn state funeral shocked the assembled dignitaries.
An audacious trick to pull

distractors.lemma: Meticulously compliant with formal etiquette.
Carefully reasoned and grounded in verified evidence.
Quietly observant without offering personal opinions.
Deeply reverent toward traditional authority.
Overly cautious when making public statements.

mnemonics: Audacious comes from Latin audere, to dare (not audire, to hear): an audacious person dares to do what others will not.

senses.definition: Spare to the point of harshness, with nothing added to please the eye or ease the body.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bare and simple in a strict, almost harsh way.

examples.text: The new memorial is austere: a single black slab with the names cut into it and no statue or flowers.
The composer's late quartets are austere, with bare lines and none of the lush harmonies of his youth.
The writer favored austere prose, with short sentences and almost no adjectives.
Next to the gilded palace, the government office looked austere, with bare floors and metal chairs.

distractors.lemma: Hard to fool, with a keen eye for what is really going on.
Of high standing and long tradition, inspiring awe.
Written or reasoned at a depth that leaves most readers lost.
Belonging to the south, especially the lands below the equator.

senses.definition: Grave and unsmiling in manner, keeping others at a distance.

mnemonics: Austere goes back to a Greek word for a dry, harsh taste; an austere room is dry in the same way, with nothing sweet or soft added.

senses.definition: Put something on record as true and stand behind it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To put your word behind a statement and stick to it.

examples.text: In his memoir, the explorer avers that he reached the summit alone, though no photo backs the claim.
The press release went on to aver that no customer data had been stolen, though it offered no proof.
Supporters of the new bridge aver that it will halve commute times, but the engineers are less sure.
My grandmother would aver to anyone who asked that her chicken soup could cure any cold.

distractors.lemma: Keep a looming harm from coming to pass.
Do some good or make a difference to an outcome.
Settle the score for an injury by hitting back at whoever caused it.
Work out to a usual figure once the highs and lows are evened out.

senses.definition: In law, set out a fact in a pleading as something one will prove.

mnemonics: Aver comes from Latin verus, true, the root of verify and veracity: to aver something is to declare it true.

senses.definition: Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Boring because everyone has heard or seen it many times before.

examples.text: The pop song relied on banal lyrics about heartbreak and summer nights that listeners had heard a thousand times.
The greeting card offered a banal verse about friendship being a gift that could have been written by anyone, for anyone.
The hotel art was banal: sunsets, sailboats and a vase of tulips hung in every single room.
The restaurant promised daring fusion food, but its menu turned out to be banal, just burgers, wings and a Caesar salad with new names.

distractors.lemma: Corrupt enough that a payment can buy one's vote, verdict or silence.
Dark and hostile in a way that makes others fear what comes next.
Remembered as a high point of success for a person or business.
Of legs, bowed so that the knees never touch.

mnemonics: Banal comes from French ban, a lord's decree: a banal oven was one the whole village had to share, so anything banal is common to everyone and has gone stale.

senses.definition: Cover up the true nature of something with an outward appearance that suggests otherwise.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something seem different from how it really is.

examples.text: Her cheerful smile belied the deep anxiety she felt about the exam results.
The shabby exterior of the restaurant belies the elegant dining room inside.
His soft, gentle voice belied a fierce determination at the negotiating table.
The calm surface of the river belies the strong currents that run underneath.

distractors.lemma: Keep hammering at an argument that everyone has already accepted.
Grieve aloud over a loss or misfortune.
Beg someone earnestly for help or mercy.
Wear someone down with a constant stream of troubles or demands.

senses.definition: Show that a claim or expectation was mistaken.

mnemonics: Belie contains lie, and comes from an old English word for deceiving: a calm face that belies your nerves tells a lie about how you feel.

senses.definition: Using one's wealth or power to do good for other people.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing good for others, often by giving them money, time or care.

examples.text: The town still honors the beneficent mill owner who paid for its library and its first hospital.
Each winter the beneficent couple quietly covered the heating bills of their elderly neighbors.
A beneficent stranger paid off every overdue school lunch account in the district, then left without giving a name.
Thanks to the will of a beneficent former pupil, the music school can now lend a violin to any child who asks.

distractors.lemma: Grand enough to make people stop and stare in admiration.
Missing some part or quantity that is needed, and so falling short.
Getting the most done for the effort and money spent.
Left in the dark about learning and progress that others enjoy.

senses.definition: Having a helpful effect, as good weather does on a harvest.

mnemonics: Bene means well and -ficent comes from facere (to do), so a beneficent act is literally doing good.

senses.definition: Add backing to something weak or under strain so that it holds up better.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prop up something weak so it stands firmer.

examples.text: The bakery added a lunch menu to bolster its weak weekday sales.
To bolster her shaky Spanish before the move, she spent a month with a host family in Seville.
Letters of thanks from former patients helped bolster the nurse's spirits after a brutal week.
A surprise win in the first game did a lot to bolster the team's shaky morale.

distractors.lemma: Talk big and loud to scare others, with nothing to back it up.
Puff oneself up in conversation to look important.
Walk out on one's own party or side without warning.
Make the skin bubble up in sore, watery patches.

senses.definition: Raise someone to sitting in bed by stacking soft supports behind them.
Fill out or line something with soft padding.

mnemonics: A bolster is a long, firm pillow that keeps you sitting up in bed; to bolster something is to give it that same steadying support.

senses.definition: Padded with grand, showy wording that hides how little is actually being said.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Puffed up with fancy words that say very little.

examples.text: His cover letter was bombastic, calling a summer of filing papers "a transformative journey in information stewardship".
Critics dismissed the novel as bombastic, full of grand speeches about destiny and very little story.
Translated into plain English, the coach's bombastic pep talk boiled down to "try harder".
The best man's toast was so bombastic, with its talk of two stars colliding across the heavens, that the guests began to giggle.

distractors.lemma: Concerned with the path a shell or bullet takes after it is fired.
Belonging to the prayerful, inward life led by monks and nuns.
Bold and harsh enough to turn a situation around at a stroke.
Mocking in tone, often by praising what one actually scorns.
Tied to classrooms, grades and the work of students.

mnemonics: Bombastic comes from bombast, cotton stuffing once used to pad out clothes: bombastic speech is padded out with grand words.

senses.definition: Crude in conduct, with the manners of someone who never learned how to behave in company.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Rude and loud, with bad manners.

examples.text: The boorish passenger in seat 14C kicked off his shoes, spread his elbows over both armrests and shouted at the crew.
He took a loud phone call in the middle of the hushed gallery, and the other visitors glared at the boorish man.
He grabbed food off other guests' plates and talked over the speeches, and his boorish behavior was all anyone discussed after the wedding.
At the interview he kept his sunglasses on, chewed gum loudly and called the manager "pal", a boorish start he never recovered from.

distractors.lemma: Known for always having a book open and a love of study.
Betting that stocks or prices are headed down.
Still having the looks or charm of a lad, even in adulthood.
Failing to hold anyone's attention for long.

mnemonics: Boorish comes from Dutch boer, a farmer: city snobs once used boor for anyone they thought had rough country manners.

senses.definition: Swell rapidly in size, number or reach, with a lively burst of new growth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To grow fast and spread out, like new leaves in spring.

examples.text: As word of the cheap rents spread, the artists' colony began to burgeon, with new studios opening every month.
Interest in home baking burgeoned during the long winter lockdowns, and flour sold out in many shops.
The city's population burgeoned from twenty thousand to half a million in just three decades.
What began as a stall at a weekend market has burgeoned into a chain of forty shops.

distractors.lemma: Bully someone into giving way through crude force or pressure.
Rob a home or office after getting in by a window or forced door.
Give way under a push or pull that has been resisted until now.
Gush out a stream of happy, jumbled talk.

senses.definition: Of a plant, push out its first buds and green shoots of the season.

mnemonics: Burgeon comes from an old French word for a bud: picture buds bursting open all over a tree in spring, and you have something that burgeons.

senses.definition: Give a claim or stance extra backing so that it stands up to challenge.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To back up an idea or plan so it is harder to knock down.

examples.text: Diaries found in an attic buttressed the historian's claim that the general had known about the plot.
New fossil finds buttress the theory that birds descended from small dinosaurs.
Two independent lab results buttressed the nurse's warning that the well water was unsafe to drink.
A string of record harvests buttressed the farmers' belief that the new seed was worth its price.

distractors.lemma: Corner someone in passing and hold them in a long, one-sided chat.
Meet a neighboring property along a shared boundary.
Charge head first into a rival to knock it off balance.
Rain blow after blow on something until it is dented or cracked.

mnemonics: Buttress comes from an old French word meaning to push against: a stone buttress pushes back against a wall, and evidence can buttress an argument the same way.

senses.definition: A din of loud, clashing sounds with no harmony between them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A harsh racket where no sound fits with any other.

examples.text: When the keeper walked in with buckets of fruit, the monkey house broke into a cacophony of shrieks and rattling bars.
Forty phones went off at once with forty different ringtones, a cacophony that stopped the lecture cold.
Construction work outside the window produced an endless cacophony of metallic clanging.
Two smoke alarms, a crying baby and a dog howling at the sirens made a cacophony that drove us out of the house.

distractors.lemma: The biggest form of classical writing for orchestra, often lasting close to an hour.
A style of writing music in which each voice carries its own tune.
Lettering drawn slowly with a broad pen or brush to be admired.
Systems that send speech down a line or over the air to a distant listener.

senses.definition: Rough, grating sounds chosen by a writer to make a line hard on the ear.

mnemonics: Cacophony comes from Greek roots kakos (bad) and phone (sound), making it a harsh noise.

senses.definition: Wear down someone's reluctance with sweet words and flattery until they agree.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To keep sweet-talking someone until they give in.

examples.text: After twenty minutes of "please" and "you're the best grandpa ever", the boy cajoled his grandfather into one more bedtime story.
The diplomat used charm and patience to cajole the reluctant leaders into signing the treaty.
By praising her past work and asking very sweetly, she managed to cajole the manager into extending her deadline.
The fundraiser knew how to cajole donors, praising their generosity so warmly that many doubled their pledges.

distractors.lemma: Sit with a grieving person and help them bear their sorrow.
Pick at tiny flaws in a plan instead of judging it as a whole.
Make a hidden deal with others to rig an outcome unfairly.
Give a shrill, gleeful laugh that grates on the ear.

mnemonics: Cajole rhymes with goal: you cajole someone with sweet talk until you reach your goal.

senses.definition: Grown so hard and unfeeling that other people's pain or misfortune stirs no pity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unmoved when others are suffering, as though the heart has gone hard.

examples.text: The driver who knocked the cyclist down sped off without a glance back, a callous act that outraged the town.
The company sent a callous letter telling the widow that her husband's pension would stop at once and asking her to return his laptop.
Her callous reply to her grieving friend, that everyone dies eventually, ended their friendship.
Even hardened reporters were shocked by how callous the warlord sounded, laughing as he described the burned villages.

distractors.lemma: Green and unseasoned, still learning how the world works.
Ending in disaster on a scale that wrecks lives or plans.
Built on lies told to blacken a rival's name.
Filled with shouting voices that will not settle down.

senses.definition: Of the palms or soles, toughened into thick pads by long wear.

mnemonics: Callous shares its Latin root, callum (hard skin), with callus: a callous heart has grown a thick, numb layer that pity cannot get through.

senses.definition: The quality of speaking one's mind plainly, without hedging or softening the truth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Telling people straight out what you really think.

examples.text: Asked what she thought of her friend's business plan, she answered with candor: the numbers did not add up and the market was crowded.
His candor set him apart from politicians who hid behind scripted, evasive answers.
With unusual candor, the coach admitted that his own poor decisions had cost the team the game.
Children are known for their candor, as anyone told by a six-year-old that their haircut looks funny can confirm.

distractors.lemma: A grudge that has soured into deep, poisonous spite.
Fiery passion that drives someone toward a person or goal.
A slow, heavy drowsiness that drains the will to move.
The din of bells, pots or steel gates crashing together.
One's standing as a contender in an election or for a post.

senses.definition: Ability to make judgments free from discrimination or dishonesty.

mnemonics: Candor shares a root with candid and candle, Latin candere, to shine: candor lets the plain truth shine through.

senses.definition: Given to abrupt reversals of mood or course that nobody can see coming.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to flip on a whim, so others never know what to expect next.

examples.text: The old boiler was capricious: some mornings it roared to life, and other mornings it sulked until noon.
The king's capricious rule meant a courtier could be honored at breakfast and banished by supper.
Fishermen on that coast respect the capricious sea, which can turn from glassy calm to whitecaps within an hour.
Small farmers are at the mercy of capricious grain prices that can double one season and collapse the next.

distractors.lemma: Roomy on a generous scale, with space to spare for whatever is put in.
Hungry for gain to the point of seizing it from others without shame.
Eager to pick holes in details that hardly matter.
Carrying good omens, as if fortune favors what is about to begin.

senses.definition: Determined by chance or impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Capricious describes actions or decisions driven by sudden whims rather than careful thought.

examples.text: His capricious decision to quit his job shocked all his colleagues.
We fell victim to the capricious whims of the tour guide.
Making large purchases on a whim is a capricious habit.
The king made several capricious decrees that confused the kingdom.
A capricious refusal
Authoritarian rulers are frequently capricious

distractors.lemma: Calculated with extreme mathematical precision.
Derived from logical reasoning and solid evidence.
Planned meticulously over a long period.
Associated with severe legal penalties.
Rooted in ancient traditions and customs.

mnemonics: A capricious person acts on a sudden caprice, shifting their mood or mind without any warning.

senses.definition: Attack someone's conduct with fierce words of blame.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To tear into someone with angry words about what they did wrong.

examples.text: The auditor's report castigated the hospital board, listing every warning it had ignored for five years.
In her review, she castigated the museum for hiding its best paintings in a basement.
Fans called the radio show to castigate the owner for trading away the team's best player.
In a scathing open letter, the scientist castigated the journal for printing a study it knew was flawed.

distractors.lemma: Get a quarrel, revolt or formal inquiry going by taking the first step.
Work a mouthful over with the teeth until it breaks down.
Gather and weigh evidence about a matter to uncover how it came about.
Take the edge off a harm or hardship so that it hurts less.

senses.definition: Inflict severe punishment on.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To castigate means to punish someone severely for wrongdoing.

examples.text: Ancient legal codes would castigate minor offenses with harsh physical penalties.
The tribunal threatened to castigate any official who accepted bribes.
Monastic rules allowed the abbot to castigate wayward monks.
Society tends to castigate those who violate core moral standards.

distractors.lemma: To heal a wound using herbal medicine.
To cast a bronze statue in a foundry.
To hide a secret treasure in a cave.
To honor a hero with a medal.
To estimate the value of a property.

mnemonics: Castigate comes from the Latin castigare, "to correct or punish": to castigate is to correct someone with harsh words.

senses.definition: Anything that sets off a shift in people or events, or hurries along one already under way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The spark that gets things moving, or moving faster.

examples.text: The factory's closure became the catalyst for a new wave of small businesses in town.
Her blunt question acted as a catalyst, and the meeting finally reached a decision.
A single viral video of the crumbling overpass became the catalyst for a statewide repair program.

distractors.lemma: An expert who breaks a market, system or problem into parts to judge how it works.
A disaster of huge scale that wrecks whole regions or societies.
A booklet or database that itemizes what a store, library or museum holds.
A church instructor who quizzes learners on a set list of beliefs until they know it by heart.

senses.definition: In chemistry, a helper substance that lowers the energy a reaction needs and can be recovered afterward.

mnemonics: Catalyst comes from the Greek katalysis, "dissolving": a catalyst breaks a fixed situation apart so that change can happen.

senses.definition: Mocking or critical with a deliberate edge that is meant to wound.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Saying harsh, mocking things that are meant to hurt.

examples.text: Her caustic reply, "Congratulations on finally reading the memo," left the whole room silent.
The editor's caustic margin notes ("Did you write this on a moving bus?") left the intern close to tears.
The comedian's caustic impressions of local politicians drew both laughter and angry letters.
Asked about his rival's new book, the professor offered a caustic one-liner: "It fills a much-needed gap."

distractors.lemma: Unplugged, producing its music with no electric pickup or speaker.
Charmingly unpolished in the manner of old farm life.
Done in an offhand, easygoing way, with little thought or ceremony.
Linking an effect to what brought it about.
Holding back and checking for danger before each step.

senses.definition: Of a chemical, strong enough to damage flesh and wear down other matter it touches.

mnemonics: Caustic comes from the Greek kaustikos, "burning": caustic words burn like acid.

senses.definition: Sly maneuvering with rules, words or paperwork to win by deceit rather than merit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sneaky tricks with rules or words that let someone cheat while seeming to play fair.

examples.text: The broker's financial chicanery, including fake invoices and shell companies, cost elderly investors their savings.
Through procedural chicanery, the senator buried the bill in a committee that was never scheduled to meet.
The landlord used legal chicanery, burying an unfair fee in the fine print, to keep tenants' deposits.
Parents cried chicanery when the school board quietly moved the meeting to a time when most of them were at work.

distractors.lemma: Gallant, gentlemanly manners that hark back to the code of medieval knights.
Effortless stylishness of the kind seen in fashion magazines.
Easy, aimless talk that passes the time between acquaintances.
Swaggering prejudice in favor of one's own nation or sex over everyone else's.

mnemonics: Chicanery comes from the French chicaner, to quibble: it means winning by sly tricks and hair-splitting arguments rather than fair means.

senses.definition: Lose the ability to flow and set into a jelly or curd, as blood does in a clot.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To thicken until it stops running and holds its shape.

examples.text: Patients on blood thinners bleed longer because their blood takes more time to coagulate.
Tofu makers stir a mineral salt into hot soy milk so that the proteins coagulate into a soft block.
The surgeon touched a heated probe to the tiny vessel so the blood would coagulate and seal it.
Rubber tappers add a mild acid to the milky latex so that it will coagulate into thick sheets.

distractors.lemma: Flock together in numbers at a shared spot, as pilgrims do at a shrine.
Puzzle away at a problem in long, silent concentration.
Recite the full set of endings a verb takes, as a language drill.
Crimp a flat sheet into a washboard pattern.
Lay down arms or drop one's objections once further resistance seems hopeless.

mnemonics: Coagulate comes from Latin coagulum, rennet, the stuff cheesemakers use to curdle milk: to coagulate is to clot or curdle.

senses.definition: Draw together from scattered pieces until they form one united thing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To slowly blend from many separate bits into one.

examples.text: Over two centuries, the scattered villages coalesced into a single sprawling city.
As the band rehearsed, stray riffs and drum patterns coalesced into the opening song of the album.
Over the summer, a handful of strangers at the community garden coalesced into a tight circle of friends.
The opposition parties failed to coalesce around one candidate, so the vote split three ways.

distractors.lemma: Give way quietly to what others want, keeping any objection to oneself.
Pass the slow stretch between leaving the sickbed and feeling fully well.
Grow faint and dissolve into thin air.
Hiss and sparkle with rising bubbles of gas.
Bully someone into going along by threatening what will happen if they refuse.

mnemonics: Coalesce comes from Latin co-, together, and alescere, to grow: separate parts grow together into one.

senses.definition: Convincing because the reasoning behind it is sound, clear and to the point.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So clear and sensible that people find it convincing.

examples.text: The defense attorney's cogent argument, built step by step on the evidence, swayed the jury.
The essay was well written but not cogent, since its conclusion did not follow from its evidence.
She made a cogent case for a four-day week, citing data from three trial programs, and the board agreed.
Unable to give a cogent reason for the delay, the contractor simply apologized.
Reviewers praised the book's cogent analysis, which left few readers doubting its conclusions.

distractors.lemma: Aware of something and keeping it in mind.
Linked by descent from a single older word or language.
Concerned with how the mind takes in, stores and uses information.
Tied to a condition, so that it stands or falls with another outcome.

mnemonics: Cogent comes from Latin cogere, to drive together or compel: a cogent argument compels you to agree.

senses.definition: Scaled to fit something else, so that the two stand in balance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fairly sized to match something else, the way a reward should match the effort.

examples.text: A quick apology was hardly commensurate with the damage his lies had done to her career.
Hikers should carry water commensurate with the length of the trail, about a liter for every two hours.
A wedding cake commensurate with a guest list of three hundred took the baker four days to finish.
Her fame as a novelist was never commensurate with her talent, and she sold few books in her lifetime.

distractors.lemma: At the very peak of skill, with nothing left to learn.
Earning respect and credit for the effort behind it.
Generous in floor space and pleasant to live in.
Benefiting from another organism's company while costing it nothing.

mnemonics: Commensurate shares a root with 'measure'; things that are commensurate have matching measures.

senses.definition: Offered in a spirit of peacemaking, to soothe an opponent and mend a rift.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Meant to cool tempers and patch things up after a fight.

examples.text: Hoping to end the strike, the company made a conciliatory offer of higher wages and an extra holiday.
After years of hostility, the two countries exchanged conciliatory gestures, freeing prisoners and reopening the border.
When her younger brother stormed off, she followed with a conciliatory plate of cookies and an offer to share the game.
After snapping at the referee, the coach jogged over with a conciliatory handshake and a quiet word of regret.

distractors.lemma: Sent or said to cheer someone's recent triumph or happy news.
Moving to and fro around a center point in a repeating cycle.
Trimmed to the essentials, with no padding in the wording.
Clashing with itself or with other accounts, so the stories do not line up.
Run as a second check to make sure a first result holds.

senses.definition: Making or willing to make concessions.

mnemonics: Conciliatory comes from Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, the root of reconcile: conciliatory words aim to reconcile.

senses.definition: Look past a wrong in a way that amounts to accepting it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To let bad behavior slide without punishing it.

examples.text: Teachers who pretend not to see the shoving in the hallway end up condoning it.
A city that never tows cars from the bike lane is, in practice, condoning drivers who block it.
Critics argued that the league's tiny fines effectively condoned violence on the field.
She condoned her husband's occasional affairs, pretending not to notice them for the children's sake.

distractors.lemma: Join someone in their sorrow by voicing comfort after a loss.
Work in favor of an outcome, making it more likely.
Cut a long text down to a tighter version.
Talk down to people, putting on an air of lofty superiority.
Puzzle someone so thoroughly that they cannot think straight.

mnemonics: Condone shares a root with donate, Latin donare, to give: when you condone a wrong, you give it a free pass.

senses.definition: A fire grown to enormous size, consuming whole streets or hillsides.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A huge fire that keeps spreading and burns down everything near it.

examples.text: The Great Fire of 1666 was a conflagration that burned much of medieval London to the ground.
Insurance adjusters walked block after block of ash, counting more than four thousand homes lost in the conflagration.
Clearing dead brush each spring helps prevent the kind of conflagration that leaps across a whole valley.
From the deck, sailors watched the conflagration light up the night sky above the burning port.

distractors.lemma: Repeated lashing of the body with a whip or knotted cord.
How the pieces of a machine, network or seating plan are laid out.
Flustered alarm that sweeps through people when plans suddenly go wrong.
The worshippers who fill the pews at a given service.
A ceremony that blesses a new church or altar for divine service.

senses.definition: A war or uprising that flares up and engulfs a whole region.

mnemonics: Conflagration comes from Latin conflagrare, to burn up, from flagrare, to blaze: a conflagration is a blaze out of control.

senses.definition: A person whose eye, ear or palate has been trained to rank fine things within one field of taste.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone with such practiced taste, say in cheese or painting, that they can tell great from merely good.

examples.text: A tea connoisseur, she sent back the pot because the water had been boiled too long.
Only a true connoisseur could spot the tiny brushwork that marked the painting as a forgery.
Casual shoppers grab the supermarket cheddar, while connoisseurs head to the back room for the cave-aged rounds.
He is no connoisseur of jazz; to him, every saxophone solo sounds the same.

distractors.lemma: A person someone turns to in private, knowing that what is said will go no further.
A person whose spoken anecdotes hold a room's attention and draw laughs.
A person who has quietly agreed with others to carry out a crime or a betrayal together.
A monarch's marriage partner, who shares the court but not the crown.
A person put into uniform by a draft order and sent wherever the army needs them.

mnemonics: Connoisseur comes from an old French word meaning to know, related to recognize: a connoisseur knows quality when they see or taste it.

senses.definition: Humbled by remorse over a fault of one's own and openly owning the harm it caused.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Ashamed of a wrong you did and ready to say so.

examples.text: Head bowed, the defendant looked contrite as he apologized to the victim's family.
The contrite teenager returned the stolen bike and offered to pay for the scratches.
After snapping at the waiter, she left a contrite note and a large tip on the table.
The company's statement sounded more defensive than contrite, and angry customers were not satisfied.

distractors.lemma: So familiar to every listener that it draws a yawn instead of a thought.
Showing the hand of its maker too clearly to feel real or spontaneous.
Buried so deep in a specialist field that only a handful of scholars can follow it.
Inclined to balk at whatever is asked of one, just to be awkward.
Pinned down in specific detail, with nothing left vague.

mnemonics: Contrite comes from Latin contritus, ground down or crushed: a contrite person feels crushed by guilt over a wrong.

senses.definition: A puzzle or problem that resists every attempt to work it out.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A question that keeps you stuck no matter how you turn it over.

examples.text: Keeping the old bridge open while building a new one beside it was a conundrum that stumped three engineering firms.
Nobody on the team could crack the conundrum of why the app ran fine on every phone except the boss's.
Why the bees abandoned a healthy hive remained a conundrum that nobody in the beekeeping club could explain.
Fitting six people, two dogs and a piano into a two-bedroom flat posed a conundrum the family argued about for weeks.

distractors.lemma: A mineral that ranks just below diamond on the hardness scale and gives us rubies and sapphires.
A team made of separate organizations that agree to fund and run an undertaking together.
A sliding scale running from one extreme to its opposite through endless in-between steps.
A hunch put forward as possibly true before anyone has the facts to check it.

mnemonics: Conundrum ends in drum: a hard puzzle keeps drumming in your head until you work it out.

senses.definition: Tangled in structure, with turns and side branches that make the main line hard to trace.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of loops and detours, so you keep losing your place.

examples.text: The museum's convoluted floor plan sent us through the gift shop three times before we found the exit.
His excuse was so convoluted that by the end nobody could remember why he had missed the flight.
The recipe was so convoluted, with sub-recipes nested inside sub-recipes, that I ordered takeout instead.
Getting a refund required a convoluted chain of phone calls, emails and signed forms.

distractors.lemma: Full of the easy good cheer that makes a party hum.
Partway back to health after a sickness, and still resting up.
Quick to talk and slow to stop, with words that come easily.
Coming from reflex or outside pressure, with no say from the person it happens to.
Marked by fits of jerking or twitching that the body cannot stop.

senses.definition: Physically bent into many tight coils or ridges.

mnemonics: Convoluted comes from the Latin convolvere, 'to roll together': a convoluted story is rolled up in so many loops that it is hard to unwind.

senses.definition: Flowing or piling up in a large, generous supply.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very large in amount, with lots of it to go around.

examples.text: The new parents received copious advice from relatives, most of it contradicting the rest.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of garlic, so buy at least two whole bulbs.
Copious footnotes, some running half a page, made the history book slow going.
Fans left copious flowers and handwritten cards outside the singer's old house, covering the whole sidewalk.

distractors.lemma: Running smoothly, with no trouble anywhere in sight.
Impossible to overlook, drawing glances from anyone nearby.
Dressed up to pass for sound reasoning when it is really a trick or an error.
Ruled by whims, so that no one can guess what comes next.
Wholehearted in religious faith and worship.

mnemonics: Copious comes from Latin copia, 'plenty', which also gives cornucopia, the overflowing horn of plenty.

senses.definition: Confirm a statement independently, so that it no longer rests on one source alone.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To back up what someone has said with proof from a second, separate source.

examples.text: Two neighbors who heard the crash were able to corroborate the driver's account of the accident.
The reporter refused to publish the claim until a second source could corroborate it.
Phone records corroborated her story that she had been at home all evening.
Letters found in the attic corroborate the family legend that their great-grandfather survived a shipwreck.

distractors.lemma: Slowly weaken a metal surface until it pits and flakes.
Team up with others on a shared piece of work.
Add more detail to an idea, plan or explanation.
Lead someone into dishonest or immoral behavior, often with bribes.

mnemonics: Corroborate and robust share the Latin robur, 'strength': to corroborate a story is to make it stronger with evidence.

senses.definition: Disposed to believe on little evidence.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to believe things without needing much proof.

examples.text: The credulous boy believed every tale his older cousins told him about a monster living in the lake.
Scam artists often target credulous investors looking for quick riches.
Only a credulous tourist would pay fifty dollars for a "genuine" Roman coin sold from a street cart.
Credulous readers shared the story about free airline tickets without ever asking where it came from.
The ad's miracle diet was so plainly fake that it could fool none but the most credulous shoppers.

distractors.lemma: Believable because it seems honest or likely to be true.
Reflecting well on whoever was responsible for it.
Working steadily and carefully without letting up.
Wavering and unsteady, especially in the voice or hands.

mnemonics: Credulous comes from the Latin credere, 'to believe', like credit and creed: a credulous person believes too easily.

senses.definition: Carried out at speed and only on the surface, with the finer points left unchecked.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick and shallow, giving something only a passing look.

examples.text: The doctor's exam was cursory: two seconds with the stethoscope and a prescription for rest.
She gave the manuscript only a cursory read before rejecting it, skipping most of the middle chapters.
The detective's search of the room was cursory, and he missed the letter taped under the drawer.
He offered a cursory apology without looking up from his phone and hurried out the door.
A cursory proofread missed the typo in the headline, which ran on the front page the next morning.

distractors.lemma: Prone to digressions, so that the main point keeps getting delayed.
Handwritten with the letters of each word linked in one unbroken line.
Struck by a hex or by fate so that misfortune follows it.
Belonging to the opening stage of a process, before the main part begins.

mnemonics: Cursory comes from the Latin cursor, 'runner', like the cursor that races across a screen: a cursory look runs past the details.

senses.definition: A supply of something so thin that people looking for it mostly come up empty.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A thin supply, with far less on hand than people want.

examples.text: The summer camp faced a dearth of lifeguards, so the lake stayed closed until August.
Given the dearth of evidence, the jury had little choice but to acquit.
Despite all the hype, the comedy suffered from a dearth of good jokes, and I laughed maybe twice.
With a dearth of letters or diaries from that century, historians can only guess how ordinary farmers felt.

distractors.lemma: The end of a life, when breath and heartbeat stop for good.
The span of something from side to side, measured apart from its length or height.
The vertical reach of a pool, well or trench below its rim.
What a borrower still has to hand back to a lender.

mnemonics: Dearth is built from dear plus -th, like warmth from warm: when food is scarce, it grows dear, meaning costly.

senses.definition: Something meant to go well that falls apart badly and in plain sight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A huge, public failure that people remember with a wince.

examples.text: The wedding was a debacle: the caterer never showed, the groom locked himself out, and the cake slid off its stand.
After the debacle of last year's picnic, when a storm blew every tent into the lake, the club booked an indoor hall.
Critics called the botched vote count a debacle that left people trusting the system even less.
The office move was a debacle: half the boxes went to the wrong city and the servers arrived a week late.

distractors.lemma: The start of a public career, marked by a first show before an audience.
An organized argument between opposing sides over a motion or policy.
A charge that lowers the balance of a bank account.
Lack of bodily strength that makes stairs and errands hard work.

senses.definition: Flooding caused by a tumultuous breakup of ice in a river during the spring or summer.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Flooding caused by broken ice rushing down a river.

examples.text: Spring brought the annual debacle that threatened the wooden bridge.
Villagers prepared their homes for the destructive river debacle.
The ice jam melted rapidly, creating a dangerous debacle.
Engineers monitored the spring debacle to prevent flooding.

distractors.lemma: A dry period of extreme heat and little rain.
A gentle shower of autumn leaves.
A thick layer of morning fog over the hills.
A calm ocean tide at midnight.
A steady stream of underground water.

mnemonics: Debacle comes from a French word for river ice breaking up: picture a frozen plan cracking apart all at once.

senses.definition: Pull apart a myth or a puffed-up claim until people see it has nothing behind it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To show that a common belief or bold claim does not hold up.

examples.text: The museum's new exhibit debunks the old myth that Vikings wore horned helmets into battle.
Two glasses of tap water and a cheap test kit were enough to debunk the salesman's claim that his filter removed every germ.
A local historian debunked the legend that George Washington slept at the inn; he never traveled that far north.
Her study debunked the idea that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.

distractors.lemma: Walk down the gangway or jet bridge when a voyage or flight ends.
Bed down for the night in a spare bed, a camp cot or a friend's couch.
Water down the worth or honor of something until it is held cheap.
Wear down the body or a group until it can barely function.

mnemonics: Debunk is de- plus bunk, short for bunkum, meaning nonsense: to debunk a claim is to strip the nonsense out of it.

senses.definition: Dignified, restrained behavior that keeps to what a solemn or formal setting expects.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Proper, dignified conduct suited to a serious or formal place.

examples.text: The judge warned that anyone who shouted again would be removed, since the courtroom demanded decorum.
Even when the groom's friends began heckling, the bride's grandmother kept her decorum and smiled politely.
Breaches of decorum at the royal court, such as turning your back on the queen, could end a career.
The rowdy fans showed little decorum, throwing popcorn and booing during the moment of silence.

distractors.lemma: The way a space has been dressed up with color and furnishings to set a mood.
An order issued from the top that people are bound to obey.
A spell of feverish confusion in which thoughts race and the mind loses its grip.
The sagging, crumbling look of a person or building far past its prime.

mnemonics: Decorum comes from the Latin decorus, 'fitting' or 'proper': decorum is behavior that fits the occasion.

senses.definition: Yielding one's own views or wishes to another person whose standing one honors.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Stepping back and letting someone you look up to have the final say.

examples.text: In deference to the hosts, who did not drink, the guests left the wine they had brought in the car.
The young chess player offered a draw in deference to the grandmaster, though she suspected she was winning.
His deference to his older brother was so complete that he never made a decision without asking him first.
The committee showed little deference to the mayor and rejected her plan outright.

distractors.lemma: Whatever sets two compared things apart from each other.
An approved pause on payments or service that would otherwise be due now.
A conclusion one reads between the lines of the facts at hand.
A gathering held to talk matters over, from a small table of partners to a packed convention hall.
Butting into matters that are not one's own and getting in the way.

senses.definition: Courteous regard for people's feelings.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being thoughtful and polite about other people's feelings.

examples.text: He lowered his voice out of deference to the sleeping infant.
She chose her words with careful deference to his sensitive nature.
His gentle reply was shaped by deference to her recent loss.
They adjusted the schedule in deference to the weary travelers.
In deference to your wishes

distractors.lemma: A strong preference for spicy food.
The act of differing from the majority opinion.
A lack of clarity in legal documents.
The careful preservation of historical artifacts.

mnemonics: Deference comes from defer, 'to yield': showing deference means you defer to someone else's wishes.

senses.definition: Damaging to health, to living things or to the proper working of something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bad for something, harming its health or how well it works.

examples.text: Years of road salt had a deleterious effect on the bridge's steel supports, which were badly rusted.
The spreadsheet error proved deleterious to the whole project, since every later estimate was built on the wrong number.
The new pesticide proved deleterious to bees, and hive numbers fell by half within a season.
Skipping sleep before an exam has a deleterious effect on memory, so cramming all night often backfires.

distractors.lemma: Mentally scrambled and agitated, so that thoughts and speech make little sense.
Good enough in flavor that diners want another helping.
Intended in advance by the person acting, who knew what they were doing.
Built so finely that rough handling would break or tear it.
Feeling a strong pull toward having or doing something.

mnemonics: Deleterious goes back to Greek deleter, a destroyer: something deleterious slowly destroys health or good working order.

senses.definition: Belittle a person, plan or piece of work with sneering, ridiculing remarks.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To mock or make fun of someone in a mean way.

examples.text: Classmates derided his homemade costume, pointing and laughing until he left the party.
Older engineers derided the first electric cars as noisy toys that no serious driver would ever buy.
Rather than offering advice, the coach derided the swimmer's form in front of the whole team, imitating her flailing arms.
He derided his sister's poetry at dinner, reading her lines aloud in a silly voice while the others laughed.

distractors.lemma: Reach a result through a chain of logical steps from a starting point.
Leave someone going without something, by taking it or holding it back.
Drive a person mad, or turn a neat arrangement into a jumble.
Fool someone, often oneself, into taking a fiction for fact.
Vandalize a surface with graffiti, scratches or splashed paint.

mnemonics: Deride comes from Latin ridere, to laugh, the root of ridicule: to deride people is to laugh them down.

senses.definition: Patterned on earlier, better-known work rather than conceived independently.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Feels like a copy of something you have already seen or heard.

examples.text: The chef's new menu felt derivative, a near copy of the dishes that had made her old boss famous.
Investors wanted something new, not another derivative app that copied a popular game.
Her early paintings were derivative of Van Gogh, right down to the swirling, thickly painted skies.
Architects grumbled that the tower was derivative, borrowing its shape and stone trim from a famous building across the river.

distractors.lemma: Valued for its looks, as trim or ornament on something else.
So thorough and trusted that later versions are measured against it.
Scornful and sneering, meant to make its target feel small.
Strikingly small, especially for a person or creature.
Given to weighing the arguments on each side in debate.

mnemonics: Derivative work is derived from someone else's: it repeats rather than creates.

senses.definition: Make something bone-dry by driving out the water it holds.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To dry something out until no water at all is left in it.

examples.text: Months without rain had desiccated the riverbed into a crust of cracked, dusty mud.
Packets of silica gel are tucked into shoe boxes to desiccate the air and keep the leather from growing mold.
Fishermen packed the cod in salt to desiccate it, so it would keep for months without rotting.
The dry winter air in the cabin desiccated our skin and lips until they cracked.

distractors.lemma: Defile a shrine, tomb or relic through an act of contempt.
Cut a population, army or group down to a small part of what it was.
Pour yourself into a single cause, task or person, holding nothing back.
Make plain that you frown on a practice or proposal.
Put an official label on a person or place, fixing what it is for.

senses.definition: Wither the spirit of a person or thing until only a husk remains.

mnemonics: Desiccate comes from Latin siccus, dry: to desiccate something is to dry it out thoroughly.

senses.definition: Gauzy and fine, so that light glows through and what lies behind shows as a faint outline.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fine and filmy, like a veil you can partly see through.

examples.text: Her diaphanous blouse needed a camisole underneath, since the thin fabric hid almost nothing.
The jellyfish was so diaphanous that we spotted it only when sunlight caught its pale rim.
The lantern's diaphanous paper shade let the candle's glow pass through as a soft haze.
The morning fog was so diaphanous that the lighthouse showed through it as a pale, ghostly outline.

distractors.lemma: Scheming and wicked in a way that seems to belong in hell.
Slanting across a shape so as to split a square into two triangles.
Musical in sound, with syllables or notes that fall gently on the ear.
Noisy in a jarring, tuneless way that sets the teeth on edge.
Tracing changes from one period to the next rather than at a single moment.

mnemonics: Diaphanous comes from Greek dia, through, and phainein, to show: a diaphanous veil lets the light show through it.

senses.definition: A sustained outpouring of furious criticism aimed at one target.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A long, furious rant that tears into a person or idea.

examples.text: Instead of offering helpful notes, the coach delivered a twenty-minute diatribe about laziness and wasted talent.
The restaurant owner answered the one-star review with a furious diatribe that insulted the reviewer's taste and manners.
Her letter to the editor began calmly but turned into a diatribe against everyone who had ever opposed the new park.
My uncle can turn any family dinner into a diatribe against modern music, shouting over anyone who disagrees.

distractors.lemma: A conversation in which each side takes turns speaking and listening.
A local variety of a language that outsiders may struggle to follow.
A heavy burden of trouble or grief that weighs on someone for a time.
A panel with the power to hear evidence and issue rulings outside the ordinary courts.
A way of reasoning in which a claim meets its counterclaim and both give way to a better idea.

mnemonics: Diatribe comes from a Greek verb meaning to wear away, and a long diatribe wears down everyone who has to hear it.

senses.definition: Written or spoken mainly to drive home a lesson, often with a heavy, lecturing hand.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Made mostly to teach a lesson, and often feels like being scolded.

examples.text: The novel grows tiresome when its didactic passages stop the story to preach about honesty.
Aesop's fables are openly didactic, each one closing with a moral spelled out for the reader.
She prefers subtle films to didactic ones that hammer home a political message in every scene.
The documentary turned didactic in its final half hour, pausing the footage so the narrator could scold viewers about recycling.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with the moment-to-moment maneuvers used to win a contest or battle.
Perceived by the fingertips rather than by the eyes or ears.
Concerned with choosing and portioning food to suit a person's health needs.
Concerned with how a sentence is built, piece by piece, from its words.
Belonging to the peak moment toward which a plot or series of events builds.

mnemonics: Didactic comes from Greek didaskein, to teach: a didactic story is written to teach a lesson.

senses.definition: Modest to the point of timidity, with too little faith in one's own powers.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too unsure of yourself to push forward or take credit.

examples.text: His diffident knock on the office door was so soft that no one inside heard it.
Being diffident, she signed her first novel with only her initials, doubting that anyone would want to read it.
On first dates he was so diffident that he answered every question about himself in a few words and then changed the subject.
A good coach can turn a diffident rookie into a player who calls for the ball with confidence.

distractors.lemma: Of another sort altogether when compared with something else.
