The coach lambasted his players at halftime, shouting that not one of them had made a tackle.
Consumer groups lambaste the airline every winter, when storms strand thousands of travelers with no information.

distractors.lemma: Keep roasting meat moist by brushing it with its own drippings.
Mourn openly, or voice sorrow over a loss.
Bond thin layers together, or seal something in clear plastic film.
Waste away, or stay stuck in a bad state with no progress.

senses.definition: Give someone a thrashing with a stick or cane.

mnemonics: Lambaste joins two old verbs, lam and baste, that both once meant to thrash. Today the thrashing is done with words.

senses.definition: Showing little energy and moving in a slow, unhurried way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Slow and lazy, with little energy.

examples.text: She gave a languid wave from the hammock, too comfortable to sit up and say hello.
By mid-afternoon the heat had made everyone languid, and nobody wanted to leave the shade.
On Sunday mornings the old dog padded around the garden at a languid pace, stopping often to lie down.
After the overnight flight, he stretched out on the sofa and gave languid, one-word answers to our questions.

distractors.lemma: Clear in thought or expression, so that it is simple to follow.
Transparent and unclouded, so that light passes through freely.
Told in gruesome or scandalous detail meant to thrill.
Long-limbed and skinny in an ungainly way.
Racked with deep suffering, in body or mind.

mnemonics: Languid comes from Latin languere, to be faint or weak, the root of languish too: a languid person seems too weak to hurry.

senses.definition: Free and lavish giving of money or gifts, often by a rich or powerful patron.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Generous giving of money or presents by someone who has plenty.

examples.text: The small museum survives on the largesse of a few collectors who cover its losses each year.
Voters grew wary of the governor's sudden largesse, which arrived as tax rebates just weeks before the election.
A tech billionaire's largesse paid for the new library wing, a scholarship fund and free summer concerts.
Tired of living on her uncle's largesse, she took a second job so she could pay her own rent.

distractors.lemma: Great size, or the fact of being bigger than most.
Theft of another person's belongings, treated as a crime.
A heavy tiredness that saps the will to do anything.
Slackness in applying rules, so that standards slip.

senses.definition: Gifts or sums of money handed out by a wealthy giver.

mnemonics: Largesse came into English from French, and its root is Latin largus, generous or plentiful: largesse is giving on a large scale.

senses.definition: Heap public attention and praise on someone, as though they were a star.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Treat someone as a hero and give them lots of attention.

examples.text: After she rescued the trapped miners, the young engineer was lionized on talk shows and magazine covers.
The tenor was lionized in Vienna, where crowds waited outside the opera house just to watch him leave.
The town lionized its quarterback, naming a street after him before he had even finished college.
Critics argue that we lionize tech founders while ignoring the engineers who actually build the products.

distractors.lemma: Give atoms or molecules an electric charge by stripping away or adding electrons.
Settle in another people's land and rule it as one's own.
Address someone in a smug tone that implies they cannot understand much.
Struggle for a long time over a hard decision or a worry.

mnemonics: Lionize comes from an old use of lion for a celebrity whom everyone wanted to see; to lionize someone is to make them that kind of lion.

senses.definition: Heavy with sorrow, in a way that often seems exaggerated.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very sad and gloomy, often more than the moment calls for.

examples.text: The undertaker spoke in a lugubrious murmur even when he was only ordering lunch.
The band followed its upbeat single with a lugubrious ballad, sung at half speed, about a widow at a graveside.
His long, lugubrious face, with drooping eyes and a downturned mouth, made strangers ask what was wrong.
Fans groaned through the coach's lugubrious press conference, where he sighed before every answer as if the season were already lost.

distractors.lemma: Promoting good health, said of air, climate or surroundings.
Slyly lewd and sexually suggestive.
Earning large profits for whoever owns or runs it.
Glowing with its own light.

mnemonics: Lugubrious comes from Latin lugere, to mourn: a lugubrious voice sounds as if it belongs at a funeral.

senses.definition: Wishing or appearing to wish evil to others; arising from intense ill will or hatred.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wanting to hurt others or to see bad things happen to them.

examples.text: Failure made him malevolent toward his old classmates, and he began spreading rumors to wreck their careers.
In the fairy tale, a malevolent fairy curses the princess to die on her sixteenth birthday.
The outage was no accident but the work of a malevolent former employee who deleted every backup on his way out.
From the doorway the old man watched us with a malevolent grin, as if he hoped we would fall.

distractors.lemma: Workable under a hammer without cracking, or easily swayed by others.
Having a strong, nasty smell.
Awkward and inept, especially in delicate situations.
Torn between two opposite feelings about something.
Weak or unhealthy from not eating enough of the right foods.

senses.definition: Having or exerting a malignant influence.

examples.text: Malevolent stars

mnemonics: Malevolent joins Latin male, badly, and volens, wishing: a malevolent person wishes others harm, while a benevolent one wishes them well.

senses.definition: Effusively or insincerely emotional.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So sentimental that it feels fake or sickly sweet.

examples.text: The film ruins a strong story with a mawkish ending, in which the dying dog wags its tail once more as violins swell.
Her editor cut the mawkish last paragraph, where the narrator weeps at a sunset and calls it her mother's final gift.
The greeting card's mawkish verse about baby angels crying happy teardrops made him cringe.
Some readers love the novel's tender scenes, but I found them mawkish and manipulative.

distractors.lemma: Quick to back war or harsh measures in dealing with other nations.
Stubbornly refusing to change course or give in.
In step with the latest trends and styles.
Scornfully making fun of someone or something.

mnemonics: Mawkish grew out of mawke, an old English word for a maggot, and first meant sickly or nauseating. Now it describes sentiment so sugary it turns the stomach.

senses.definition: Someone who dislikes people in general.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who does not like or trust other people and keeps away from them.

examples.text: A lifelong misanthrope, the old lighthouse keeper said he preferred gulls to people because gulls never asked questions.
Her neighbors called her a misanthrope because she never answered the door and scowled at anyone who waved.
The sitcom's hero is a misanthrope who moves to a remote island so he never has to speak to another human being.
Years of reading online comment sections can turn even a cheerful person into a misanthrope.

distractors.lemma: Someone who stockpiles money and begrudges every cent spent.
Someone who holds women in contempt.
Someone who studies how human cultures and societies developed.
Someone sent abroad by a church to spread its faith.

mnemonics: Misanthrope joins Greek misein, to hate, and anthropos, human being: a misanthrope hates humankind.

senses.definition: A small or moderate or token amount.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just a little of something, often barely enough.

examples.text: If he had shown even a modicum of remorse, the judge might have given him a lighter sentence.
The report adds only a modicum of new data; most of it repeats last year's findings.
With a modicum of planning, you can avoid most of the stress of moving house.
The climbers set off without even a modicum of caution, ignoring the storm warning posted at the trailhead.

distractors.lemma: A separate unit that can be fitted together with others to build something larger.
The habit of playing down one's own talents or achievements.
An official pause on some activity, ordered for a set time.
The force a moving thing gathers that keeps it going.

mnemonics: Modicum comes from modicus, the Latin for moderate, which is built on modus, a measure: a modicum is a modest measure of something.

senses.definition: Sharp and stinging in a way meant to wound, especially in humor or criticism.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Funny or critical in a harsh, biting way that hurts.

examples.text: Chefs dreaded her mordant reviews, which could empty a new restaurant within a week.
The play's mordant take on office life had the audience laughing and wincing at the same time.
Even in his last letters, Twain kept his mordant wit, mocking the greed and hypocrisy he saw around him.
Her mordant remark that the committee had finally achieved nothing at record speed stung everyone in the room.

distractors.lemma: Preoccupied with dying, disease and decay in a way that seems unwholesome.
Fading toward its end, with little life or energy left.
Quietly at rest for a period, with its activity paused rather than ended.
Full of guilt and sorrow over your own past wrongdoing.

mnemonics: Mordant comes from Latin mordere, "to bite": mordant humor bites. Dyers use the same word for a chemical that makes color bite into cloth.

senses.definition: Head off a difficulty in advance, so that some later action is no longer required.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something unneeded by dealing with the problem ahead of time.

examples.text: A second backup drive would obviate the need to rebuild every file by hand after a crash.
Writing a clear contract at the start can obviate months of argument later on.
The new bridge obviated the long ferry ride that commuters had made for decades.
She packed snacks and games for the children to obviate any meltdowns on the long drive.

distractors.lemma: Cloud the meaning of something on purpose, often to hide the truth.
Make someone answerable for doing something, through a law, contract or promise.
Turn aside from the expected path, plan or standard.
Cut a written word down to a few of its letters.

mnemonics: Obviate shares Latin via, "way," with obvious: you meet a problem in the road ahead and clear it, so no fix is needed later.

senses.definition: So hateful or offensive that it fills people with disgust.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Horrible in a way that makes people feel disgust and hate.

examples.text: Charging grieving families double for funeral flowers struck everyone as an odious way to make money.
The regime's odious policy of jailing children along with their parents drew protests around the world.
Most voters found the candidate's jokes about wounded veterans odious and punished him at the polls.
Slavery was defended for centuries, though we now see it as one of the most odious institutions in history.

distractors.lemma: Having a scent strong enough to notice.
So dull and slow that time seems to drag.
Pleasant to hear because of its tuneful sound.
Hinting that bad things lie ahead.

mnemonics: Odious comes from Latin odium, "hatred," which English also uses for strong public dislike. Odious things earn odium.

senses.definition: Harden into a fixed state that no longer changes or lets in new ideas.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To get stuck in old ways and stop changing or growing.

examples.text: Without new members, the club's traditions ossified, and every meeting followed the same script for thirty years.
Critics warned that the party had ossified into a circle of aging leaders who no longer listened to voters.
Some novelists ossify after an early success and write the same book again and again.
The company let its sales methods ossify while younger rivals kept testing new ideas online.

distractors.lemma: Keep alternating between two positions or moods without coming to rest.
Cut someone off from a group by treating them as if they were not there.
Combine with oxygen, which is what makes iron rust.
Lower the pH of a substance so that it turns more sour and corrosive.

senses.definition: Turn into bone, or harden into bony tissue.

mnemonics: Ossify comes from Latin os, "bone": an ossified mind has gone as stiff as bone.

senses.definition: A formal tribute, spoken or written, that heaps praise on a person or achievement.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Glowing praise of someone, spoken aloud or written down.

examples.text: The retiring coach sat red-faced through a twenty-minute panegyric in which the team captain praised every season he had led.
Instead of a balanced history, the author produced a 600-page panegyric that praised every decision her subject made and skipped every failure.
Critics wrote panegyrics to the young pianist after her debut, calling her the finest talent of her generation.
At public festivals, Roman orators delivered panegyrics on the emperor's wisdom and victories.

distractors.lemma: A funny copy of a well-known work or style, made to poke fun at it.
A small unbound booklet handed out to argue a cause or spread information.
A rewording of a passage that leaves its sense intact.
A show in which actors tell a story with gestures and no spoken lines.

mnemonics: Panegyric comes from Greek panegyris, a gathering of all the people (pan, "all"): it was praise spoken before the whole crowd.

senses.definition: A person who is shunned and looked down on by a group or by society as a whole.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person everyone avoids or refuses to accept.

examples.text: After the cheating scandal, the once-popular senator became a pariah whom no colleague would be seen with.
Countries that break the treaty risk becoming international pariahs, cut off from trade and aid.
When she reported her own company's fraud, she became a pariah in the industry and could not find another job.
In the novel, the villagers treat the orphan as a pariah and cross the road to avoid him.

distractors.lemma: One of the people a parish priest or minister looks after.
An elder man whose authority his relatives or followers accept.
A figure hailed as the one who will save a nation or cause.
A person whose love for their homeland leads them to stand up for it.

mnemonics: Pariah comes from Tamil paraiyar, "drummers," a caste in southern India that others long treated as outcasts.

senses.definition: Showing contempt or a low opinion, especially through the choice of a word or name.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Said in a way that puts someone or something down.

examples.text: Calling the plan "cheap" sounded pejorative, while calling it "affordable" would have sounded like praise.
The word "bureaucrat" is often pejorative, suggesting someone who cares more about rules than results.
Once a neutral word for a farm worker, "villain" took on a pejorative meaning over the centuries.
The style guide tells reporters to avoid pejorative nicknames and to call groups by the names they use for themselves.

distractors.lemma: Issuing orders in a curt tone that shuts down any objection.
Going through the motions, with no real effort behind it.
Causing damage slowly and quietly, so that the harm is noticed late.
Serving to get things ready for what comes next.

mnemonics: Pejorative comes from Latin pejor, "worse": a pejorative word makes something sound worse than it is.

senses.definition: Always on the move, living or working in one place after another.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Moving around a lot and rarely staying in one place for long.

examples.text: As a peripatetic nurse, she drove to a different village clinic every day of the week.
Because of his father's army postings, he had a peripatetic childhood, moving between eight schools in ten years.
The band's peripatetic schedule took it to a new city almost every night of the tour.
After retiring, the couple sold their house and took up a peripatetic life in a camper van.

distractors.lemma: Off at the edges of an area or issue, not at its core.
Stirring pity, or so feeble that it earns scorn.
Exposing someone to serious danger.
Turning out to foretell what later happened.

senses.definition: Belonging to the school of philosophy that Aristotle founded.

mnemonics: Peripatetic comes from Greek peripatein, "to walk around" (peri, "around"). Aristotle's pupils got the name from the covered walk where he taught.

senses.definition: By nature cool and unhurried, with feelings that seldom rise to the surface.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Steady and unruffled, rarely showing much feeling at all.

examples.text: Even when the engine caught fire, the phlegmatic pilot read out the checklist in the same flat voice he used for weather reports.
She took the news of her layoff with a phlegmatic shrug, as if she had been told it might rain.
The striker's phlegmatic manner meant he never celebrated a goal, but simply jogged back to the center circle.
Her phlegmatic husband showed no sign of joy at his surprise party, nodding to the guests as if it were an ordinary Tuesday.

distractors.lemma: Judging ideas mainly by whether they work in real life.
Holding to a set of doctrines so rigidly that no evidence can shift them.
Delivered with strong stress so that the point cannot be missed.
Done openly and shamelessly, making the wrongdoing impossible to overlook.

mnemonics: Phlegmatic comes from phlegm, one of the four body fluids that old doctors thought shaped a person's temper. Too much phlegm was said to make a person slow and calm.

senses.definition: Words or applause that publicly praise someone for an achievement.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Praise or cheers that people give someone who did well.

examples.text: The young surgeon won plaudits from senior staff for staying calm through a twelve-hour operation.
Despite the plaudits from critics, the film made little money at the box office.
The mayor took the plaudits for the new park, though volunteers had done most of the work.
Her first novel earned plaudits in every major newspaper and a place on the prize shortlist.

distractors.lemma: A stock phrase people fall back on when they have nothing real to say.
How believable an account or excuse sounds when you first hear it.
A short tryout performance for a role, band or choir.
A close review of account books by an outside examiner.

mnemonics: Plaudit comes from Latin plaudite, "applaud!", which Roman actors called to the audience at the end of a play.

senses.definition: Forbid a practice through a law, decree or other official rule.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To ban something officially.

examples.text: After two wildfires last summer, the city's new code proscribes fireworks within a mile of the forest.
Medical boards proscribe romantic relationships between doctors and their patients.
The treaty proscribes chemical weapons, and any country caught using them faces sanctions.
School rules proscribe phones in class, so teachers collect them at the door.

distractors.lemma: Write an order for a drug that a doctor wants a patient to take.
Mark letters permanently on a hard object, often as a record or dedication.
Say that a result was brought about by a certain person or factor.
Sign up for a service or magazine that bills you on a schedule.

senses.definition: Publicly name someone as an outlaw, putting their life and property at risk.

mnemonics: Proscribe comes from Latin proscribere, "to post publicly": Roman leaders posted the names of people they declared outlaws. Link PROscribe with PROhibit.

senses.definition: Prone to grumbling and fault-finding, with a sour, easily irritated temper.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always complaining in a cranky, whiny way.

examples.text: By the third hour of the drive, the querulous passenger had complained about the music, the heat and every stop.
The querulous patient pressed the call button every ten minutes to report that the soup was cold, the room too bright or the nurse too slow.
Help desk staff learn to stay patient with querulous callers who find fault with everything.
Her letters grew querulous in later years, full of grievances about neighbors, doctors and the weather.

distractors.lemma: Chasing noble dreams with little thought for whether they can come true.
Always ready to chat, and slow to stop once started.
Having an unsettled stomach and a sense of nausea.
Trembling and unsteady in pitch, usually from age or strong emotion.

mnemonics: Querulous comes from Latin queri, "to complain," which also gave English the word quarrel. A querulous person always has a complaint ready.

senses.definition: Greedy in a grasping, ruthless way, seizing whatever wealth can be had.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So greedy that you take money or goods from others without caring who gets hurt.

examples.text: The rapacious landlord raised the rent three times in one year and kept every tenant's deposit.
Rapacious traders stripped the island of its sandalwood within a decade, leaving the hills bare.
Critics accused the firm of rapacious tactics: it loaded each company it bought with debt and sold off the pieces.
The invading army was rapacious, seizing grain, livestock and anything else the soldiers could carry.

distractors.lemma: Generous in size, with room for plenty of contents.
Expressing delight so great that it seems almost dreamlike.
Nursing a lasting hatred toward someone over a past wrong.
Harsh and noisy in a way that grates on the ears.
Wholly caught up in what one is watching or hearing.

senses.definition: Living by hunting and eating other animals.

mnemonics: Rapacious comes from Latin rapere, "to seize": a rapacious person seizes whatever they can get.

senses.definition: Formally reject or disavow a formerly held belief, usually under pressure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To publicly take back something you said or believed, often because you are forced to.

examples.text: Facing a heresy trial, the astronomer chose to recant rather than risk being burned at the stake.
The key witness later recanted, admitting that police had pressured him to name the defendant.
Even under torture, the poet refused to recant a single line of his attacks on the regime.
Years later the senator recanted her earlier defense of the war and called her vote a grave mistake.

distractors.lemma: Narrate an experience, going through what took place step by step.
Rebuild or rewrite something so that it is organized differently.
Move wine from its bottle into a carafe so that the dregs stay behind.
Withdraw from hearing a case because personal ties could bias one's decision.
Flinch away quickly from something that shocks or disgusts.

mnemonics: Recant comes from Latin re-, "back", and cantare, "to sing": to recant is to sing your old words back, taking them back.

senses.definition: Strongly suggesting something else, so that it calls that thing to mind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Strongly reminding you of something, the way a scent can bring back a place or time.

examples.text: The old hotel, with its brass elevators and velvet curtains, is redolent of the 1920s.
The campaign's backroom deals were redolent of the machine politics of a century earlier.
Her speech was redolent of the civil rights era, echoing the rhythms of the great preachers of that time.
The novel's first chapters are redolent of Dickens, full of orphans, fog and cruel schoolmasters.

distractors.lemma: Lazy by habit and fond of doing nothing.
Openly rude to people one is expected to respect.
Repeating what is already there, and so unnecessary.
Gleaming and grand to look at, with rich colors or fine dress.
Holding back from telling others what one thinks or feels.

senses.definition: Heavy with the odor of a particular thing.
Giving off a sweet, pleasant scent.

mnemonics: Redolent comes from Latin olere, "to smell", also found in olfactory: a redolent scene smells of another time and brings it to mind.

senses.definition: Confidently optimistic and cheerful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Expecting things to turn out well, even when the odds look poor.

examples.text: Even after a third failed launch, the engineers stayed sanguine, sure the fix was only weeks away.
Few economists are sanguine about a quick recovery while unemployment keeps rising.
She was sanguine about the surgery, joking with the nurses and planning a hiking trip for the spring.
Investors who were sanguine in January had grown nervous by March, after six straight weeks of losses.

distractors.lemma: Marked by heavy slaughter, or eager for it.
Acting holier than others in a smug, preachy way.
Clean and free of the germs or dirt that spread disease.
Regarded as beyond challenge, so that no one dares alter it.
Making fun of things with dry, bitter scorn.

senses.definition: Having a ruddy, healthy-looking complexion.
Of the deep red color of blood.

mnemonics: Sanguine comes from Latin sanguis, "blood": medieval doctors believed people ruled by blood were cheerful and hopeful.

senses.definition: Seeming reasonable until it is looked at closely, and then proving false.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sounding true or sensible at first, but wrong when you look more carefully.

examples.text: The lawyer's specious argument fell apart once the jury saw the security footage.
It is specious to claim that the new law cut crime just because crime fell the year after it passed.
The ad made the specious promise that a single pill could replace diet and exercise.
His excuse sounded convincing at first, but the editor soon saw that it was specious and full of holes.

distractors.lemma: Roomy and open, with no sense of being cramped.
Pinned down to one exact item, case or detail.
Catching the eye at once because it is unlike what surrounds it.
Pale and shadowy in the manner of a ghost.
Out of the ordinary and given extra value or attention.

senses.definition: Based on pretense; deceptively pleasing.

mnemonics: Specious comes from Latin species, "appearance": a specious argument has the look of truth and nothing more.

senses.definition: Openly scornful of others out of a belief in one's own superiority.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Looking down on others with cool pride, as though they are not worth your time.

examples.text: His mother eyed my clothes with a supercilious air, as if I had shown up in pajamas.
The supercilious waiter sniffed when we asked whether the house wine came by the glass.
She gave the intern a supercilious smile and one raised eyebrow, then went on talking as if he had said nothing.
Some critics take a supercilious tone toward popular novels, as if anyone who enjoys them must be a little dim.

distractors.lemma: Dealing only with the outside of things and never going deeper.
Present in excess, adding nothing that is needed.
So excellent that nothing else comes close to it.
Worn out or pushed aside because of old age.
Exact about rules and manners, down to the smallest point.

mnemonics: Supercilious comes from Latin supercilium, "eyebrow": a supercilious person looks down on others with one eyebrow raised.

senses.definition: Unspoken, yet understood and observed by everyone involved.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Agreed on or known by all without a single word being said about it.

examples.text: By saying nothing when the plan was announced, the board gave its tacit approval.
The two neighbors had a tacit agreement: neither mentioned the fence, and neither moved it.
Her silence was taken as tacit consent, though she later said she had simply been too stunned to speak.
Nobody ever said so aloud, but there was a tacit rule among the staff that no one went home before the boss did.

distractors.lemma: Seldom willing to talk, and quiet by nature.
Perceived through contact with the hands or skin.
Chosen for its immediate advantage in a fight, game or contest.
Skilled at handling touchy matters without hurting anyone's feelings.

mnemonics: Tacit comes from Latin tacere, "to be silent": a tacit agreement is one made in silence.

senses.definition: Rash boldness that ignores danger or what is considered proper.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The nerve to do something bold that others find rude or unwise.

examples.text: The new intern had the temerity to tell the CEO, in front of the whole staff, that her plan would fail.
After losing every match this season, he had the temerity to demand a raise.
One reporter had the temerity to interrupt the general mid-sentence and call his answer a lie.
She was stunned by the temerity of a stranger who walked into her kitchen and helped himself to the fridge.

distractors.lemma: Stubborn persistence in pursuing a goal despite setbacks.
A habit of never overindulging, especially in alcohol.
A readiness to flare up in anger at small things.
Great quickness in getting something done.

mnemonics: Temerity comes from Latin temere, "blindly" or "rashly": temerity is boldness that charges ahead without looking.

senses.definition: Felt through another person's experience instead of one's own.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Enjoyed or suffered through another person's adventures, as if they were your own.

examples.text: Reading her sister's letters from Paris gave her a vicarious taste of life abroad.
Some parents seek vicarious glory through their children's sports, shouting louder than anyone on the field.
Fans feel a vicarious thrill when their team wins the title, though none of them threw a single pass.
Reality shows offer viewers a vicarious glimpse of a luxury they will never live themselves.

distractors.lemma: Meaning to hurt others, savagely and on purpose.
Differing from one another and more than one in number.
Bubbly and lively in a way people find appealing.
Shaky and in danger of failing or falling at any moment.

senses.definition: Suffered or done by one person as a substitute for another.

examples.text: Vicarious atonement

mnemonics: Vicarious shares a Latin root with vicar and vice president, people who stand in for someone else: a vicarious thrill is felt in someone else's place.

senses.definition: Savagely bitter and hostile in what is said or written.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of spiteful, angry words meant to wound.

examples.text: The senator's vitriolic attack on her rival included insults about his family and his looks.
The restaurant closed weeks after a vitriolic review called the chef a fraud and the food inedible.
Comments under the article grew so vitriolic that the newspaper shut them off within an hour.
Their divorce turned vitriolic, with each side calling the other a liar in court and in the press.

distractors.lemma: Glassy in texture, or actually made of glass.
Felt secondhand, by sharing in what happens to someone else.
Spoiled in quality, or made legally void by a defect.
Fired at such heat that clay or rock melts together into a dense, waterproof solid.

senses.definition: Able to burn or eat away other substances by chemical action.

mnemonics: Vitriolic comes from vitriol, an old name for sulfuric acid: vitriolic words burn like acid.

senses.definition: Making one's views heard in a loud, insistent way, again and again.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Speaking up noisily and often about what you believe, so no one can miss it.

examples.text: The plan to close the library met vociferous opposition, with residents packing every council meeting for months.
She was a vociferous critic of the dam, writing letters, giving speeches and leading marches against it.
A vociferous crowd outside the stadium chanted the coach's name until he came out to wave.
Even his most vociferous defenders fell silent when the recordings were played in court.

distractors.lemma: Hungry for huge quantities, whether of food or of anything else.
Truthful in speech, never bending the facts.
Taking up a great deal of space, or running to many pages.
Teaching the practical skills of a trade instead of academic subjects.

mnemonics: Vociferous comes from Latin vox, "voice", and ferre, "to carry": vociferous people make their voices carry.

senses.definition: Willing to be bribed or to sell one's honor for money.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Easy to bribe, and ready to bend any rule for enough cash.

examples.text: The venal police officer let the smugglers pass in exchange for a fat envelope of cash.
Voters were tired of venal officials who handed out building permits to whoever paid the most.
The judge proved venal, quietly accepting gifts from the very companies whose cases he heard.
Historians describe the old royal court as venal, a place where titles and pardons were openly for sale.

distractors.lemma: Small enough to be pardoned without much fuss.
Typical of the season between winter and summer.
Found in or flowing through the veins.
Having to do with punishing people who break the law.
Stale and predictable from having been said or done too many times.

mnemonics: Venal comes from Latin venum, "sale", the root of vendor: a venal official is up for sale.

senses.definition: Someone who gathers around a powerful figure as an admirer and does that figure's bidding.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An admirer who stays close to an important person and does whatever they ask.

examples.text: The famous chef arrived surrounded by acolytes who carried his knives and wrote down every word he said.
Every summer the aging painter invited a few acolytes to his studio, where they mixed his paints and copied his style.
As a young acolyte of the director, she fetched coffee, read scripts and studied how he worked with actors.
The guru never answered questions himself; one of his acolytes always stepped forward to speak for him.

distractors.lemma: Someone newly won over to a religion or cause from a different one.
Someone just starting out in a field, with little practice yet.
Someone who takes part with another person in breaking the law.
Someone who chooses a life of hardship, going without comfort and pleasure.

senses.definition: An assistant at a church service who carries candles or serves at the altar.

mnemonics: Acolyte comes from Greek akolouthos, meaning a follower or attendant: an acolyte follows a leader around.

senses.definition: Go along with a plan or demand without objecting, despite private doubts.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give in and let something happen, even though you'd rather it didn't.

examples.text: After weeks of arguing, the landlord finally acquiesced and let the tenants keep their cat.
The board acquiesced to the merger, although several members privately thought it was a mistake.
Tired and outvoted, he acquiesced in the group's choice of restaurant rather than start another fight.
The workers would not acquiesce to longer shifts without a raise, so they voted to strike.

distractors.lemma: Set a defendant free at the close of a trial by finding them not guilty.
Give someone first-hand knowledge of a subject, place or person.
Take ownership of something, whether through purchase, effort or a gift.
Merge from separate parts into a single united body.
Spend time resting and growing stronger after being sick or hurt.

mnemonics: Acquiesce comes from Latin acquiescere, to rest or be at peace (quies, rest, as in quiet): when you acquiesce, you stay quiet instead of objecting.

senses.definition: Praise and worship heaped on someone far beyond what is reasonable.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Over-the-top praise and admiration, the kind fans pour on a pop star.

examples.text: The young pitcher was not ready for the adulation that followed his perfect game, with fans camping outside his house.
After years of adulation from critics, the novelist was stunned when her new book was mocked.
The dictator's portrait hung in every classroom, and children learned songs of adulation for him.
She found the crowd's adulation embarrassing and slipped out the back door after the concert.

distractors.lemma: Making food or medicine impure by mixing in cheaper or harmful substances.
Ritual cleansing of the face, hands and feet before prayer.
Copying a rival's methods in the hope of matching or outdoing them.
A long, high, wavering cry used to mourn or to celebrate.
A smooth rising and falling motion or shape, as of waves or hills.

mnemonics: Adulation comes from Latin adulari, to fawn or flatter: adulation is the fawning praise a crowd heaps on its hero.

senses.definition: Support and oversight from an organization or person that lends its name and authority to something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The backing and protection of a powerful group or person that stands behind a project.

examples.text: The peace talks took place under the aegis of the United Nations, which supplied the venue and the mediators.
The festival grew from a small street fair once it came under the aegis of the city's arts council.
Under the aegis of a powerful senator, the young aide's bill finally reached a vote.
The study ran under the aegis of the national health service, which paid for it and checked its methods.

distractors.lemma: A route or a right to exit from an enclosed space or property.
A close reading that draws out what a sacred or classic passage means.
The way in which a thing first came about, from its earliest stage.
Bias against people on account of their age, often aimed at older workers.

senses.definition: In Greek myth, a shield belonging to Zeus that Athena also carried into battle.

mnemonics: In Greek myth the aegis was a protective shield carried by Zeus and Athena, so working under someone's aegis means working under their shield.

senses.definition: Open to a suggestion or request and ready to go along with it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Ready to say yes to an idea or a request when someone asks.

examples.text: The landlord was amenable to a later move-in date as long as we paid the first month's rent up front.
If the client is amenable to the change, we can push the meeting to Friday and finish the report first.
Most of the staff were amenable to the new schedule once they learned it meant shorter Fridays.
He is usually stubborn, but after a good dinner he becomes far more amenable to suggestions.

distractors.lemma: Pleasant company because of a warm and cheerful temper.
Able to be changed or corrected after it was first written.
Full of romantic longing toward another person.
Lowly and repetitive, the sort of work that earns little pay or respect.

senses.definition: Able to be handled or tested by a particular method.
Bound to obey a particular court, ruler or set of rules.

mnemonics: Amenable comes from French amener, to lead or bring: an amenable person can be led to agree.

senses.definition: Someone who openly abandons the religion or political creed they used to hold.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person who quits their religion or beliefs and turns against them.

examples.text: Once a leading voice in the movement, he was branded an apostate after he published an essay rejecting its ideas.
In some countries, an apostate who leaves the state religion can be sent to prison.
Her old party treated her as an apostate when she switched sides and ran against its candidate.
The parish records describe him as an apostate who had abandoned the faith of his parents.

distractors.lemma: Someone who, in past centuries, made up and sold medicines from herbs and minerals.
Someone who rules a land with power that nobody can check.
Someone on trial as a newcomer to a convent or monastery, before taking any vows.
Someone who presides over a local court for petty crimes and small claims.

mnemonics: Apostate comes from Greek apostasis, a standing away (apo, away, and stasis, standing): an apostate stands away from a faith.

senses.definition: Suited to the subject being discussed or to what is happening at the time.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just right for what is being talked about or what is going on.

examples.text: Her joke about lost luggage was especially apropos, since half the guests had just arrived without their bags.
Given the storm raging outside, the choir's song about rain seemed oddly apropos.
I found his remark about patience apropos, because we had already waited two hours for the train.
The professor chose an apropos quotation about failure to open the class right after the midterm results came out.

distractors.lemma: Said to have happened, though no reliable record backs the story up.
Warning of a disaster so vast that it would bring the world to an end.
Ordinary and flat, with nothing in it to stir the imagination.
Belonging to one company, which stops others from copying or using it.
Near enough to the true figure to be useful, though a little off from it.

mnemonics: Apropos comes from the French phrase à propos, meaning to the purpose: an apropos remark is to the point. The phrase apropos of means speaking of.

senses.definition: A person or body whose judgment on a question is accepted as final.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The person or group whose decision settles a question for everyone else.

examples.text: For decades the magazine was the arbiter of what counted as good taste in fashion.
On questions about the Constitution, the Supreme Court acts as the final arbiter.
When the twins fought over toys, their grandmother acted as arbiter, and nobody argued with her ruling.
Critics are no longer the only arbiters of a film's success now that audiences post their own reviews.

distractors.lemma: A trained worker who prunes trees and keeps them healthy.
In Britain, a lawyer qualified to plead cases before senior judges.
Someone who urges on or backs another person's wrongdoing.
Someone who makes furniture, pottery or other goods by hand with great skill.

senses.definition: Someone picked by two sides to hear their quarrel and settle it.

mnemonics: Arbiter is a Latin word for a judge, and it shares a root with arbitrate: an arbiter settles the question.

senses.definition: A position of control in which one side holds sway over its rivals.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being on top, with more power or influence than your rivals.

examples.text: By the end of the war, the northern kingdom had gained ascendancy over all of its neighbors.
The two factions fought for ascendancy within the party until the younger one took over the leadership.
Once the reformers won ascendancy on the board, they rewrote the company's rules within a month.
The general's ascendancy over the weak king meant that every royal order really came from him.

distractors.lemma: A spiritual condition that rises above everyday human life.
A condition of being put on hold, waiting to be taken up again.
The act of naming a particular cause or author as the source of something.
A head count of those present at an event, a class or a meeting.

mnemonics: Ascendancy comes from Latin ascendere, to climb up: a group in the ascendancy has climbed to the top.

senses.definition: Cause something to lose strength or impact without removing it entirely.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To turn down the strength of something so it has less effect.

examples.text: Thick curtains attenuate the noise from the street, so the bedroom stays fairly quiet.
The drug does not cure the disease, but it can attenuate the worst of the symptoms.
Over the years, distance attenuated their friendship until they spoke only once a year.
Engineers fitted dampers to attenuate the swaying that had made people nervous on the bridge.

distractors.lemma: Give sworn or written backing to a claim, confirming it is genuine.
Adjust one's mind or habits until they match a place or a group.
Repair the harm of a past wrong or sin through one's own deeds.
Switch on a mechanism or set its moving parts working.

senses.definition: Thin out a gas or liquid so that it becomes less dense.
Make a germ or virus less harmful, as when preparing a vaccine.

mnemonics: Attenuate comes from Latin tenuis, thin, the root of tenuous: to attenuate something is to thin it out.

senses.definition: Use charm or flattery to lead someone into a false belief or a bad choice.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To trick someone by being so charming that they let their guard down.

examples.text: The con artist beguiled lonely retirees with flattering letters before asking them for money.
Don't let the salesman's easy smile beguile you into signing a contract you haven't read.
Investors were beguiled by the founder's tales of overnight riches, none of which turned out to be true.
The cult leader beguiled new members with promises of peace, then took control of their savings.

distractors.lemma: Feel bitter that someone else got a reward or a lucky break.
Produce a child as its father, or bring a result into being.
Sneer at what someone has done and deny it any credit.
Settle in writing which heirs will get one's estate once one has died.

senses.definition: Enchant someone and keep them pleasantly absorbed.

mnemonics: Beguile contains guile, meaning sly cunning: to beguile someone is to work your guile on them.

senses.definition: Left without something one needs or prizes, usually because it has been lost.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Missing something important that you once had or badly need.

examples.text: After the factory closed, the town was bereft of jobs, and its main street slowly emptied.
Critics called the remake bereft of ideas, since it copied the original scene for scene.
Bereft of his notes, the speaker stumbled through the first few minutes of his talk.
The rocky island, bereft of fresh water, could never support a permanent village.

distractors.lemma: Under a debt of gratitude to someone and so not free to act against them.
Kept in ignorance and clinging to old, backward beliefs.
Muddled in the head and losing track of what is going on.
Caught up in a violent frenzy that no one is able to calm.
Soaked and messy, with hair and clothes hanging limp after rain or mud.

senses.definition: Grief-stricken and desolate after a death or a parting.

mnemonics: Bereft is the old past form of bereave, from an Old English verb meaning to rob: someone bereft of hope has been robbed of it.

senses.definition: A tight band of insiders working in secret to seize or hold on to power.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A small secret group that schemes behind the scenes to gain control.

examples.text: A cabal of senior managers met privately each week and settled promotions long before the official reviews took place.
Historians argue that a small cabal of nobles plotted in secret to remove the young king's chief adviser.
The new editor discovered that a cabal of board members had been quietly steering the paper's coverage.
Several founders formed a cabal within the company, plotting in whispers behind the chief executive's back to push him out.

distractors.lemma: The circle of top department heads who meet with a leader to shape policy.
A ceremonial ride through the streets by a troop of horsemen.
A gathering of a party's local members to vote on whom to back for office.
A body of people hired to fill a theater and applaud on cue.
A set of people tracked together in a study because they started in the same year.

senses.definition: A covert plan, hatched by a few, to do harm or break the law.

mnemonics: Cabal reached English through French cabale, a word for hidden knowledge, and a cabal keeps its plans hidden from everyone outside its small circle.

senses.definition: Treating serious things lightly, with a careless, superior air.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting as if something serious is no big deal.

examples.text: The manager's cavalier attitude toward safety rules ended when a worker was hurt on the loading dock.
He was strangely cavalier about the overdue tax bill, tossing it into a drawer unopened.
Critics attacked the senator's cavalier remark that a few lost jobs were a fair price for progress.
Her cavalier treatment of borrowed books, returned dog-eared and coffee-stained, annoyed the library staff.

distractors.lemma: Ruled by whims, so that moods and plans shift without warning.
Vast and hollow, with a deep, echoing space inside.
Gaunt, hollow-cheeked and pale as a dead body.
Bold in battle or hardship, refusing to back down.

mnemonics: Cavalier comes from Italian cavaliere, a horseman: picture a rider who looks down from the saddle and brushes off whatever happens below.

senses.definition: Embarrassment mixed with irritation, felt when a plan goes wrong or one is made to look foolish.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The annoyed, embarrassed feeling you get when something goes wrong or you end up looking foolish.

examples.text: To her chagrin, the cake she had boasted about all week collapsed as she carried it to the table.
Much to the coach's chagrin, his team gave up three late goals a day after he boasted that they never lost a lead.
He hid his chagrin with a joke when the waiter loudly announced that his card had been declined.
The mayor's chagrin was plain when reporters pointed out the spelling mistake on the city's new welcome sign.

distractors.lemma: Sly, tricky dealing meant to fool people, often by bending legal rules.
Aggressive, flag-waving loyalty to one's own side that sneers at outsiders.
A show of make-believe that fools almost nobody who is watching.
A look of pain or distaste that screws up the whole face for a moment.
A harsh scolding handed out to set someone straight after misbehavior.

mnemonics: Chagrin ends in grin, but it is the stiff, forced grin you put on when you are embarrassed and annoyed.

senses.definition: Hem in by setting firm limits on what is allowed or possible.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To limit how far something can go or what someone is allowed to do.

examples.text: The new rules sharply circumscribe what campaign groups may spend in the final month before an election.
Her role was circumscribed from the start: she could advise the board but never vote.
A tight budget circumscribed the museum's plans, and the new wing shrank to a single gallery.
Doctors warned that his illness would circumscribe his travel, keeping him within an hour of a hospital.

distractors.lemma: Dodge a rule or barrier by taking a crafty side route.
Make a voyage that goes right round the globe and returns to its starting port.
Spread through a group, handed along from one member to the next.
Write out a recording or speech word for word on paper or screen.
Name a cause, author or source as the one behind something.

senses.definition: Mark out an area by tracing a line around its edge.
Draw one figure around another so that it touches at points without crossing it.

mnemonics: Circumscribe comes from Latin circum, around, and scribere, to write or draw: you draw a line around something, and it may not cross it.

senses.definition: Occurring with or following as a consequence.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Happening along with something else, often as a side effect of it.

examples.text: The town's rapid growth came with concomitant problems, from traffic jams to a shortage of school places.
The drug eases pain, but drowsiness is a concomitant effect that many patients dislike.
Fame and its concomitant loss of privacy took the young singer by surprise.
Rising seas bring flooding along with them, and coastal towns are bracing for that concomitant threat.

distractors.lemma: In fair proportion to something else.
Touching along a shared edge with nothing in between.
Meant to soothe anger and win back goodwill.
Exactly as harsh as the wrongdoing deserves.
Having plenty of room inside.

mnemonics: Concomitant comes from Latin con, with, and comes, companion: a concomitant effect travels with something as its companion.

senses.definition: Scheme secretly with others toward a dishonest or harmful end.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To secretly team up with others to do something sneaky or wrong.

examples.text: The two clerks connived to move small sums into a hidden account over several years.
Historians believe the king's brother connived with foreign envoys to seize the throne.
She suspected her siblings had connived to cut her out of their father's will.
Several players connived with gamblers to lose matches on purpose.

distractors.lemma: Hint at an extra shade of meaning beyond the dictionary sense.
Open up about private worries to a listener one trusts.
Send goods to an agent who will store them or sell them.
Shake with sudden jerks that cannot be controlled.

mnemonics: Connive comes from Latin connivere, to shut the eyes or wink: conspirators wink at one another, or shut their eyes to the crime.

senses.definition: Having or revealing supreme mastery or skill.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So skilled at something that it is hard to imagine anyone doing it better.

examples.text: A consummate diplomat, she could calm two furious delegations with a few well-chosen words.
The pianist was a consummate performer, playing the fiendish piece without once glancing at the keys.
Even rivals admitted he was a consummate craftsman, able to carve in an afternoon what took others a week.
Only a consummate host could make a dinner for forty guests look so effortless.

distractors.lemma: Done at once, skipping the usual formal steps.
In step or harmony with something else.
Careful and dutiful, never cutting corners.
Reached by general agreement rather than by a vote.
Openly scornful of someone thought unworthy.

senses.definition: Complete and perfect, lacking nothing.
Total and utter, often of someone who fits a bad type through and through.

mnemonics: Consummate comes from Latin summa, the total, from summus, highest, the root of summit: a consummate artist has reached the top of the craft.

senses.definition: Act in breach of a law, treaty or set of rules.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To break a rule or law instead of following it.

examples.text: Selling the medicine without a license would contravene federal law.
The company's new hiring policy may contravene the union contract it signed last year.
Referees ruled that the extra padding contravened league rules on equipment.
By firing on the convoy, the rebels contravened the ceasefire they had agreed to only days before.

distractors.lemma: Summon a board or panel to sit for a formal session.
Step in to change how someone else's quarrel ends.
Engineer an outcome through craft or cunning.
Turn something over in the mind for a long while.

senses.definition: Argue against or deny the truth of a claim.

mnemonics: Contravene comes from Latin contra, against, and venire, to come: to contravene a rule is to come up against it head-on.

senses.definition: A select little circle that keeps close company and shuts out others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A few friends or fans who stick close together and keep others out.

examples.text: The poet shared her drafts only with a small coterie of trusted friends.
A coterie of wealthy collectors snapped up the painter's work before it ever reached the gallery walls.
Newcomers found it hard to break into the coterie of regulars who held the same corner table every Friday.
The director cast the same coterie of actors in film after film, rarely giving outsiders a chance.

distractors.lemma: A slow line of mourners following a coffin.
A circle of witches who gather to practice their craft.
A firm whose members are also its owners.
Several firms pooling money and skill for one big project.
A group sent from one place to join a larger gathering.

mnemonics: Coterie goes back to French cote, a hut, the root of cottage: picture a few friends in their own little cottage with the door shut to outsiders.

senses.definition: Allow or go along with something, or give it one's approval.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To be willing to accept or allow something.

examples.text: The principal said she would not countenance bullying of any kind.
Her parents refused to countenance the idea of her dropping out of college.
The board would never countenance a merger that cost so many local jobs.
The old general could not countenance retreat, even when his officers begged him to fall back.

distractors.lemma: Withdraw a command so that it no longer has to be followed.
Push back against an effect until it fades or disappears.
Forge money or branded goods so they pass as genuine.
Fight or vie with rivals for a prize or position.

mnemonics: Countenance is also an old word for a face: to countenance a plan is to show it an approving face instead of a frown.

senses.definition: Cowardly in a spineless, shameful way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So scared of trouble that you act in a weak, shameful way.

examples.text: The craven captain fled in a lifeboat while passengers were still trapped below deck.
Critics called the senator's silence craven, since he privately agreed the policy was wrong but feared losing donors.
In a craven surrender, the general handed over the city without firing a single shot.
Too scared to face the angry customer, he made a craven exit through the back door and left his intern to cope.

distractors.lemma: Coarse and blind to what is fitting.
Sneaky and quick to outwit others.
Hungry enough to eat almost anything.
Grumpy and quick to snap at people.
Easily taken in, trusting claims without proof.

mnemonics: Craven sounds a lot like cave in, and a craven person caves in the moment courage is called for.

senses.definition: Lower oneself, with an air of superiority, to do something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To grudgingly do something you feel is too lowly for someone of your rank.

examples.text: The star did not deign to answer reporters' questions and swept past them into her car.
After weeks of silence, the landlord finally deigned to reply, sending a one-line email.
The head chef rarely deigned to speak to the kitchen porters.
Would the champion deign to play a match against a club amateur?

distractors.lemma: Fake an emotion or an injury so as to mislead.
Hold an opinion about what something is or how good it is.
Sit on the throne and govern a kingdom.
Formally quit a post before one's term is up.
Declare a ruler or hero to be a god.

mnemonics: Deign comes from Latin dignari, to think worthy, from dignus, worthy, the root of dignity: you deign to do a task you think barely worthy of you.

senses.definition: A political figure who gains power by inflaming the public's resentments and telling crowds what they want to hear.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A leader who wins over crowds by playing on what they fear and hate.

examples.text: The demagogue blamed every hardship in town on newcomers, and the crowd cheered each accusation louder than the last.
Ancient Athens had its share of demagogues, and Cleon swayed the assembly with fiery attacks on the rich.
Give a gifted demagogue a bad harvest and a convenient villain, and a crowd's grumbling soon becomes fury.
The editorial warned that hard times make voters easy prey for any demagogue who offers enemies to blame instead of plans.

distractors.lemma: A schoolteacher, often one who insists on rules and corrects every small slip in a lesson.
A hero of myth with some divine blood, mightier than any mortal yet short of godhood.
A researcher who tracks a population's births, deaths, ages and movements over the years.
A person who follows one fixed theory so rigidly that every fact gets bent to fit it.

mnemonics: Demagogue comes from Greek demos, the people, and agogos, leader: a demagogue leads the people by playing on their fears.

senses.definition: A person or creature that lives in a certain spot, or haunts it so often that it seems to belong there.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person who lives somewhere, or turns up there so often that they seem part of the place.

examples.text: The night-shift nurses had become denizens of the hospital cafeteria and knew every cook by name.
Anglerfish and other strange denizens of the deep ocean live their whole lives without sunlight.
A longtime denizen of the library's reading room, he had a favorite chair that no one else dared to take.
Pigeons, rats and raccoons are the hardiest denizens of the city's back alleys.

distractors.lemma: A veteran who, after the longest career in a field, is treated as its elder.
A person whose open criticism of those in power can cost them their freedom or their home.
A man who makes his tailored suits and careful grooming the center of his life.
A senior academic who oversees the teachers, budgets and students of one college within a university.

senses.definition: A plant or animal from elsewhere that has settled in and now grows wild in a new region.

mnemonics: Denizen comes from Old French deinz, inside: a denizen is someone inside a place and at home there, never just a visitor.

senses.definition: Standing to gain or lose nothing from how a matter turns out, and therefore impartial.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Free of any personal stake, and so able to be fair to both sides.

examples.text: The two companies agreed to let a disinterested engineer, paid by neither side, decide whose design caused the collapse.
Because she owned no shares in either firm, the judge could weigh the merger dispute as a disinterested outsider.
A disinterested referee would have called the foul, but the coach's own brother was holding the whistle.
The scholarship committee brought in disinterested readers who had never met any of the applicants.

distractors.lemma: Putting on a show of frankness while keeping back what one really knows.
Turned against a leader or group one used to back, and sullen about it.
Stripped of an earlier faith in something after seeing its flaws up close.
Robbed of hope and courage by a setback or a string of failures.

mnemonics: Disinterested is dis-, meaning not, plus interest in its old sense of a stake, as in conflict of interest: a disinterested umpire has nothing riding on the game.

senses.definition: Grim and unsmiling, giving off a heavy, cheerless air that keeps others at a distance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Serious and unsmiling in a way that makes someone seem cold and gloomy.

examples.text: The dour landlord read the lease aloud without once looking up or cracking a smile.
Even at his daughter's wedding, the dour old farmer managed only a stiff nod.
Her dour expression made the new interns too nervous to ask a single question.
Known for his dour manner, the coach surprised everyone by bursting into laughter at the team dinner.

distractors.lemma: Wearing plain, out-of-date clothes that do nothing for one's looks.
Built to stand up to hard use for years without wearing out.
Pleasant and soothing to hear, with a soft and sweet tone.
Faithful in prayer and worship, and earnest in one's religious belief.
Alive but inactive for a period, waiting for conditions to change.

senses.definition: Grimly stubborn and unwilling to give any ground.

mnemonics: Dour probably comes from Latin durus, hard: picture a dour face as hard as stone, never softening into a smile.

senses.definition: Funny in a quiet, offbeat way, often delivered with a straight face.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Funny in a quiet, slightly odd way that makes people smile rather than laugh out loud.

examples.text: With a droll glance at the empty buffet table, the host declared the dinner a great success.
His droll remarks during the dull budget meeting kept the whole table quietly grinning.
The museum guide had a droll habit of describing the stuffed animals as if they were retired staff.
She delivered the droll punch line without a hint of a smile, which only made it funnier.

distractors.lemma: Dull and colorless, with nothing bright to catch the eye.
Heavy with sleep and struggling to keep one's eyes open.
Sagging limply, as if too tired to hold itself up.
Sweeping and severe in effect, going well beyond the usual measures.

mnemonics: Droll comes from French drôle, funny or odd: a droll remark is funny in an odd, quiet way.

senses.definition: Explain a puzzling point or idea in enough detail that others can understand it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To explain a hard idea so that other people can finally follow it.

examples.text: The professor drew a simple diagram to elucidate how the heart's four chambers work together.
Asked to elucidate his vague remarks, the spokesman only repeated them more slowly.
The footnotes elucidate the old legal terms that most modern readers would not recognize.
Letters found in the attic helped elucidate why the two sisters had stopped speaking for thirty years.

distractors.lemma: Wind up a bankrupt firm, auctioning its stock and equipment so creditors get something back.
Coax an answer or a response from someone through careful questions.
Promote someone to a loftier post, or set something on a higher level.
Treat a hinge, gear or engine with oil or grease to stop it sticking.

mnemonics: Elucidate comes from Latin lucidus, bright, the root of lucid: to elucidate an idea is to make it bright and clear.

senses.definition: Having filled a certain role or held a certain status in the past, but no longer.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Describing what someone or something used to be, but is not anymore.

examples.text: The erstwhile factory, turned into lofts ten years ago, still has its old loading docks and freight elevator.
The erstwhile allies, who had once shared a trench, ended the war as bitter enemies.
The town's erstwhile mayor now drives a school bus and seems much happier for it.
The erstwhile train station now houses a small museum of local history.

distractors.lemma: Deeply sincere, meaning every word with no hint of a joke.
Rewarding enough to justify the work or expense it takes.
Shifting course or mood without warning, with no steady pattern.
Deeply learned as the fruit of years of wide reading and study.

mnemonics: Erstwhile joins erst, an old word for formerly, with while: your erstwhile friend was your friend a while ago.

senses.definition: Let a feeling or trait be plainly seen through what one says or does.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give clear signs of an emotion or trait, often without putting it into words.

examples.text: The young pianist evinced remarkable calm, playing on through a broken string without missing a beat.
The witness's shaking hands evinced a fear that her steady voice tried to hide.
Few of the students evinced any interest in the lecture, and several were openly asleep.
The letters evince a deep affection between the two painters that their public quarrels never hinted at.

distractors.lemma: Remove renters from a home or shop by order of a court.
Bring someone around to believing an argument or claim.
Flinch, with a quick tightening of the face, at a sudden pain.
Dodge a duty, a question or a pursuer instead of facing it.

mnemonics: Evince comes from Latin evincere, to prove: when your face evinces surprise, it proves to everyone that you are surprised.

senses.definition: Having lasted into the present, when others of its kind were lost or destroyed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Still around today, when you might expect it to have been lost or destroyed.

examples.text: Of the playwright's forty comedies, only eleven are extant; the rest are known only by their titles.
The coelacanth, long thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, turned out to be very much extant.
Only three copies of the first printing are still extant, and one of them sits in a library in Edinburgh.
Crocodiles belong to one of the oldest extant groups of reptiles on Earth.

distractors.lemma: Openly jubilant over a victory or a stroke of good fortune.
Eagerly on the lookout for something one believes will come soon.
Lying outside the subject under discussion and adding nothing to it.
Costing so much more than it should that buyers feel cheated.

mnemonics: Extant comes from Latin exstare, to stand out or exist: extant species are still standing, unlike extinct ones.

senses.definition: Reached with too little thought, and so shallow and oversimplified.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too quick and simple to take seriously, as if no real thinking went into it.

examples.text: The report offered the facile conclusion that students fail only because they are lazy.
Telling someone with depression to "just cheer up" is facile advice that ignores how the illness works.
Critics found the film's ending facile, since it settled twenty years of family conflict with a single hug.
The debate coach warned that facile slogans, which skip every hard part of the issue, would cost them points with the judges.

distractors.lemma: Doomed to come to nothing, however hard anyone tries.
Delicate enough that a knock or a drop would ruin it.
Making light of things at a moment that calls for seriousness.
Liable to drop a friend or a cause on a whim and take up another.

senses.definition: Done with the smooth, practiced ease of a skilled performer.
Able to speak or write with easy fluency.

mnemonics: Facile comes from Latin facilis, easy, as in facility: a facile answer came too easily to be any good.

senses.definition: Loyalty owed and pledged to a lord, ruler or leader, often under a formal oath.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A promise to stay loyal to someone in power, like a knight's promise to his lord.

examples.text: Kneeling before the king, each knight swore fealty and promised to fight whenever called.
In return for the land, the farmer owed fealty to the baron and a share of every harvest.
New members of the council were expected to show fealty to the chairman by voting as he told them.
The rebel lords refused to pledge fealty to the young queen, and the kingdom slid toward civil war.

distractors.lemma: Feebleness of body or will, often seen in the very old.
Land, together with the buildings on it, held as property.
An argument that seems sound but rests on a flaw in its reasoning.
A grave offense against the law that can bring years in prison.
A loss of life in a crash, a fire, a war or a similar event.

mnemonics: Fealty comes through Old French from Latin fidelitas, the root of fidelity: fealty is faithfulness sworn to a lord.

senses.definition: Sly and stealthy, in the manner of someone hoping to go unnoticed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sneaky and secret, like someone who hopes nobody is watching.

examples.text: During the exam he cast furtive glances at his neighbor's paper whenever the proctor looked away.
Keeping low and silent, the cat made a furtive approach to the kitchen counter while the cook's back was turned.
With a furtive look over her shoulder, she slipped the letter into the drawer and locked it.
The two employees held furtive meetings in the stairwell, where no manager ever went.

distractors.lemma: Made up for a story, with no existence outside it.
Burning with strong, sincere feeling about a belief or cause.
Wildly angry, to the point of shouting or lashing out.
Coming about through luck or accident, with no one arranging it.

mnemonics: Furtive comes from Latin fur, thief: a furtive glance is the quick, guilty look of a thief.

senses.definition: Socially clumsy and tactless, through inexperience or a lack of polish.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Clumsy with people, and likely to blurt out a tactless remark or break an unspoken rule.

examples.text: It seemed gauche to ask the bride how much the wedding had cost, so I kept quiet.
At his first formal dinner, the nervous teenager made the gauche mistake of tucking his napkin into his collar.
Her gauche joke about the host's divorce brought the conversation to an icy halt.
Surrounded by such polished guests, I felt gauche, as if I had wandered in straight from a barn.

distractors.lemma: Loud and flashy in color or ornament, to the point of looking cheap.
Wasted to the point that the cheekbones jut out and the cheeks sink in.
Light, thin and so sheer that one can almost see through it.
Irritating in a way that stings one's pride and lingers.

mnemonics: Gauche is French for left: an old prejudice held that left-handed people were clumsy, so gauche came to mean socially awkward.

senses.definition: Draw the borders of election districts so that one party ends up with an unfair edge.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To redraw voting maps on purpose so that one party is sure to win more seats.

examples.text: Critics say the ruling party gerrymandered the state so cleverly that it kept most seats while losing the popular vote.
Lawmakers tried to gerrymander the city by splitting one neighborhood of opposition voters across four districts.
A federal court threw out the new map, ruling that it had been gerrymandered to weaken the votes of Black residents.
Because district lines are redrawn every ten years, whichever party controls the legislature at that moment gets a chance to gerrymander.

distractors.lemma: Begin to sprout, as a seed does once it has water and warmth.
Follow a looping, wandering path instead of going straight.
Carry on a string of casual romances while being unfaithful.
Throw away money or a chance through careless spending or use.
Seize a vehicle or building for official use without asking its owner.

mnemonics: Gerrymander joins Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who signed an 1812 voting map, with salamander, the shape one twisted district on that map seemed to have.

senses.definition: Said or speaking with an easy fluency that glosses over how hard or serious a matter really is.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Smooth and quick with words, but too easy and shallow to be trusted.

examples.text: Asked how the city would pay for the new stadium, the mayor said only that 'the money will be found,' a glib remark that satisfied no one.
The tutor's glib advice to 'just relax' did nothing for a student who had already failed the exam twice.
His glib summary of the war, 'the good side won,' skipped over a decade of hard and costly choices.
Critics disliked the film's glib ending, in which a lifelong family feud is settled with a single hug.

distractors.lemma: Visibly low in spirits, with a long face and a heavy, drooping manner.
Bubbling over with merry high spirits, sometimes in a mischievous way.
Icy toward others, holding back any sign of warmth or welcome.
Of eyes or a stare, blank and dull, as if nobody were behind them.

mnemonics: Glib is related to old Dutch and German words for slippery: glib talk slides smoothly past the hard parts of a question without getting a grip on them.

senses.definition: Plagued by bad luck, so that plans and efforts keep ending badly.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unlucky, with things going wrong again and again.

examples.text: The hapless chef dropped the wedding cake, set off the fire alarm and then locked himself out of the kitchen.
Every time the hapless goalkeeper dived one way, the ball seemed to bounce the other.
In the comedy, a hapless inventor watches each of his machines fall apart at the very moment buyers arrive.
The hapless team has lost its last twelve games, several of them in the final minute.

distractors.lemma: Left to chance, with no system guiding how things were arranged.
Posing no danger, so that nobody needs to fear it or guard against it.
Charging ahead while ignoring the risks that others point out.
Made in a rush, before the facts have been properly weighed.

mnemonics: Hapless is hap, an old word for luck or chance (still heard in happen and mishap), plus -less: a hapless person is without luck.

senses.definition: Theatrical in a way that blows feelings far out of proportion, as if playing to a crowd.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Making a big, showy fuss about your feelings, more than the situation calls for.

examples.text: She wept and wrung her hands over a tiny scratch on her car door, a histrionic scene staged mainly for the neighbors.
The coach's histrionic protest, complete with a thrown clipboard and a fall to his knees, earned him a fine.
Critics said the mayor's histrionic speech, full of shouting and fist-pounding, hid how little the plan would change.
Toddlers can be histrionic, wailing as if the world has ended when a cracker breaks in half.

distractors.lemma: Marking a turning point that earns a lasting place in the record of the past.
Bold beyond the ordinary, standing firm against danger that would make most people flee.
Unusually shaggy, with a thick growth of hair that is hard to miss.
Clinging to custom so stubbornly that any change looks like a threat.

senses.definition: Having to do with the theater and the craft of performing in plays.

mnemonics: Histrionic comes from Latin histrio, an actor: a histrionic person acts out every feeling as if on a stage.

senses.definition: Intrude upon a right, a resource or a person's time so that less of it is left.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To intrude on something, like your rights or your free time, and leave you with less of it.

examples.text: Civil liberties groups argued that the new airport scanners impinge on the privacy of every passenger.
She refused to let late-night work emails impinge on the evenings she kept for her children.
Judges must decide whether the law impinges on free speech or only limits where protests may be held.
Officials warned that the cost of the new stadium would impinge on the money set aside for schools and parks.

distractors.lemma: Cast public doubt on a person's honesty or on the truth of a claim.
Push a person into doing something, as fear or duty might.
Run a pointed pole or spike right through a body or an object.
Lock up a car, goods or papers on the orders of a court or the police.
Hand on knowledge, news or a quality to someone or something.

senses.definition: Strike or land on a surface, as a beam of light or a jet of water does.

mnemonics: Impinge comes from Latin impingere, to drive or push into: whatever impinges on your rights pushes into them.

senses.definition: Openly question whether a person can be trusted or whether a claim holds up.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say in public that someone's motives or statements are dishonest or wrong.

examples.text: Rather than answer the charges, the mayor tried to impugn the reporter, calling her a paid tool of his rivals.
The ad campaign set out to impugn the candidate's honesty by digging up a decades-old expense scandal.
Rival officers impugned the general's loyalty after he met in secret with the enemy's envoy.
No reviewer could impugn the study's findings, since every step had been checked twice by outside labs.

distractors.lemma: Lay the blame for a mistake or misdeed at someone's door.
Seize goods or a vehicle by official order and hold them in a guarded lot or store.
Cut into someone's time, space or liberty in an unwelcome way.
Spur someone on to do something, giving them a strong urge to act.

mnemonics: Impugn comes from Latin impugnare, to fight against (pugnare, to fight, as in pugnacious): to impugn a claim is to fight it.

senses.definition: Cutting quickly to the core of a problem with clear and pointed reasoning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sharp and clear, going straight to what matters most.

examples.text: In one incisive paragraph, the reviewer showed exactly why the novel's twist made no sense.
The editor's incisive notes cut my rambling draft down to the three arguments that actually mattered.
A short, incisive memo on the budget pinpointed the two programs that were driving the deficit.
Known for her incisive mind, the detective spotted the one detail in the alibi that did not add up.
